tools.name: query_resource
tools.description: Read any listed DreamGraph resource with canonical identity, evidence, revision, currency, completeness and whole-record continuation. Follow every cursor before claiming complete retrieval. Empty matches are successful empty results; invalid/unavailable resources are explicit errors. Runtime and graph capability URIs have distinct meanings.

uri.description: Registered resource URI. system://capabilities describes runtime; system://capability-entities contains project capabilities.

filter.description: Top-level entity payload fields; strings match case-insensitively. The same filter is required on continuation.

limit.description: Maximum whole records per page (1–1000; default 50). Byte limits may return fewer.

max_bytes.description: Maximum serialized page bytes including metadata (1024–65536; default 8192). Individual records are never clipped or skipped.

cursor.description: Opaque continuation from the same URI/filter/revision. Changed state, daemon restart, scope change or expiry requires restarting the query.

contract_version.description: v1 returns revisioned record pages; legacy is an explicit bounded presentation adapter without paging.

tools.name: read_source_code
tools.description:
Read source code from a file. **Entity mode is the primary path** in DreamGraph; line-range and full-file are fallbacks.
1. **Entity mode** (always prefer): pass `entity` to read a specific function, class, interface, type, enum, or class method by name. Returned verbatim.
2. **Line range mode** (fallback): pass `startLine`/`endLine` when no named entity fits. Returned verbatim.
3. **Full file mode** (last resort): omit both. May be clipped with a head/tail preview for very large files.

If you don't know the exact entity name, use `query_api_surface` first, or `search_source_code` as a fallback discovery aid, then re-run in entity mode.

filePath.description: File path relative to the project root (e.g. 'src/server/webhooks/maventa.ts') or an absolute path.

repo.description: Repository name. Available: "dreamgraph". Path is resolved relative to this repo root.

entity.description: Name of a code entity to extract (function, class, interface, type, enum, or const). When provided, returns only the source code of that entity including its JSDoc/decorators. Examples: 'registerCodeSensesTools', 'ChatPanel', 'EditorContextEnvelope'. Overrides startLine/endLine when provided.

startLine.description: Start line (1-based). If provided, returns only a portion of the file.

endLine.description: End line (1-based, inclusive). If provided together with startLine, returns only that range.

Replace the entire source code of a named entity (function, class, interface, type, enum, or const) in a source file. The tool finds the entity by name, determines its boundaries (including JSDoc/decorators), and replaces it with the provided new source code.

**Workflow:** First use `read_source_code(entity=...)` to see the current implementation, then use `edit_entity` to replace it. This is safer and more token-efficient than `edit_file` with large old_text/new_text blocks.

tools.name: patch_file
tools.description: Apply multiple find-and-replace edits to a single file in one atomic operation. Each edit is `{ old_text, new_text }` and is applied sequentially in the order given. If ANY edit fails (no match, ambiguous match, write error) the file is left unchanged. Strongly preferred over multiple `edit_file` calls when patching large markdown plans, design docs, or any file with ≥3 edits in the same pass — it cuts payload overhead (no repeated file context) and guarantees all-or-nothing semantics.

old_text.description: Exact text to find. Must match exactly one location at the moment this edit is applied (i.e., after all earlier edits in this batch). Include 3-5 lines of surrounding context to ensure uniqueness.

new_text.description: Replacement text. Empty string deletes the match.

edits.description: Array of edits applied sequentially. All-or-nothing.

tools.name: edit_markdown_section
tools.description: Replace the body of a markdown section identified by its heading. The heading line itself is preserved unless `include_heading=true`. occurrence.description: Which matching heading to target when multiple sections share the same heading. 1-based. Default 1 (first match).

decisions.title: Defend graph purity by separating durable plans from adaptive operational graph cognition

context.problem: Standalone Architect plans and implementation slices need permanent historical preservation, but completed workflow/task cognition must not remain indefinitely active in the DreamGraph. If every completed task, slice, checkpoint, and execution instruction stayed in the active graph forever, retrieval and reasoning would accumulate stale context and the underlying LLM would drown in obsolete operational detail instead of seeing current project reality.
constraints: Markdown plans under plans/ are durable project artifacts and must remain preserved after completion.
Per-plan implementation logs are mandatory for auditability, user visibility, and crash/power-outage recovery.
The DreamGraph prioritizes active project understanding, durable operational state, accepted architecture, verified capabilities, and current implementation reality.
Temporary execution workflow structures are useful during active implementation but become harmful when they continue to participate in active cognition after stabilization.
Historical evidence must remain available through markdown plans, implementation logs, ADR history, provenance, and archived evidence even when temporary graph workflow entities fade.
Graph RAG and Architect context assembly must avoid overloading the LLM with stale completed-task context.

decision.chosen: Plans remain as permanent markdown-backed historical artifacts, while graph workflow cognition is adaptive and temporary. During active work, plans may be operationalized into graph workflow entities such as plan nodes, slice nodes, gates, continuation state, checkpoints, candidate futures, and execution entities. As work completes and stabilizes, those temporary structures must crystallize into durable project knowledge by creating, mutating, enriching, superseding, merging into, or removing durable entities such as Feature, DataModel, Workflow, API, Capability, Tool, UIRegistryElement, ADR, and related project-state entities. Completed implementation instructions should not remain indefinitely active as future execution cognition.

alternatives.option: Keep every plan, task, slice, checkpoint, and implementation step permanently active in the graph.
alternatives.rejected_because: This preserves detail but pollutes operational cognition, increases stale retrieval, and risks drowning the LLM in obsolete execution context.

alternatives.option: Remove completed plans and logs once graph entities are updated.
alternatives.rejected_because: This destroys the permanent historical project record and undermines auditability, reasoning traceability, and crash/recovery continuity.

alternatives.option: Store plans only in the graph and not in markdown.
alternatives.rejected_because: This makes historical artifacts dependent on graph lifecycle policies and conflicts with DreamGraph markdown-backed planning practices.

alternatives.option: Never create temporary workflow graph entities for plans.
alternatives.rejected_because: This avoids graph cleanup but loses useful active coordination, review gates, continuation state, and graph-aware implementation support during execution.

expected: Plans and implementation logs remain permanently available under plans/ as historical evidence.
The active graph remains focused on current durable project reality instead of completed execution instructions.
Planning tools must distinguish temporary workflow state from durable project entities.
planning:sync_plan_graph and planning:archive_plan must support crystallization and fading of completed workflow cognition.
Graph RAG context quality should improve by avoiding retrieval of stale completed slices as if they were active work.
Users retain visibility into implemented vs unimplemented plan parts through markdown logs even after workflow graph structures are archived or removed.
risks: Crystallization bugs could remove useful workflow context before durable entities are correctly updated.
Over-aggressive graph cleanup could make resume behavior worse if implementation logs are incomplete.
Under-aggressive cleanup could still allow stale execution cognition to pollute retrieval.
Entity mapping from slices to durable graph concepts may require human review for ambiguous plans.

guard_rails: Do not delete or discard markdown plans or their implementation logs after completion.
Do not keep completed plan slices, checkpoints, or execution instructions indefinitely active in the graph once they have stabilized.
Before fading temporary workflow entities, crystallize verified results into durable project entities or record why no durable graph change is appropriate.
planning:archive_plan must preserve historical markdown artifacts and provenance while reducing active graph workflow noise.
planning:get_resume_packet must prefer the live implementation log and current durable project state over stale completed workflow entities.
Graph RAG and Architect context assembly should prioritize durable project entities and active plan state, not archived completed-task cognition.
Any implementation that treats the graph as the sole historical store for plans violates this decision.

decisions.title: Standalone Architect plan operational state is daemon-owned and crystallizes into durable graph knowledge

context.problem: The migration plan required a decision on where active plan state lives. Without an explicit rule, implementation could fragment state across sidecar JSON, browser-local business state, markdown-only mutation, or permanently-active graph execution structures.
constraints: ADR-142 requires markdown plan narrative plus ADR/graph-readable mirrors, not markdown alone.
ADR-207 requires permanent markdown preservation while keeping active graph cognition adaptive and temporary.
Current slice, status, checkpoints, gate outcomes, continuation state, run traces, and pending review state need daemon-owned coordination so resume behavior survives browser reloads and UI restarts.
UI-local state such as layout, focus, and selection may remain browser-local, but durable operational state must remain authoritative in DreamGraph-owned records.

decision.chosen: Lock active standalone Architect plan state to daemon-owned DreamGraph operational records and graph workflow cognition during active execution, while preserving markdown plans and append-only implementation logs as the durable historical record. Active state may include current slice, status, checkpoints, gate decisions, continuation state, task/run traces, and pending review projections. As work stabilizes, temporary workflow cognition must crystallize into durable project entities or fade from active cognition per ADR-207.

alternatives.option: Persist active plan state primarily in browser storage or a frontend-only cache
alternatives.rejected_because: This breaks crash/reload continuity and makes the browser the accidental source of truth for operational state.

alternatives.option: Keep all plan state only in markdown files
alternatives.rejected_because: Markdown is the historical narrative record, not the sole coordination substrate for active plan execution and checkpoints.

alternatives.option: Keep completed execution structures permanently active in the graph
alternatives.rejected_because: ADR-207 rejects permanent active cognition for completed slices because it pollutes retrieval with stale execution detail.

expected: Resume packets and plan status can be reconstructed from daemon-owned operational records plus append-only markdown logs.
The browser stays a projection/control surface rather than a business-state owner.
Implementation can distinguish between historical plan artifacts and active coordination state without inventing sidecar persistence silos.
risks: Entity mapping from active slices to durable graph updates may still require careful implementation review.
If daemon-owned state and markdown logs drift, resume UX may become confusing until synchronization tooling matures.

guard_rails: Do not store authoritative active plan execution state exclusively in browser-local storage or frontend-only caches.
Do not treat markdown plans as the only operational state store for checkpoints, continuation, or review state.
Do not keep completed plan execution structures indefinitely active once their verified outcomes have crystallized into durable project entities.
Do not introduce a separate sidecar persistence model for core operational plan state unless a future ADR explicitly justifies it.

decisions.title: Cognitive lifecycle state machine is the authoritative orchestration model

context.problem: The system contains multiple cognitive modes and transitions, but no recorded ADR explains why the lifecycle exists or what invariants future changes must preserve.
constraints: Cognitive operations are stateful and may have long-running side effects
Dreaming, normalization, lucid exploration, nightmare scanning, and discipline ingest must remain distinguishable
Future changes by humans or agents need guard rails to avoid invalid state transitions

decision.chosen: Treat the explicit cognitive lifecycle states (including AWAKE, REM, NORMALIZING, NIGHTMARE, LUCID, and INGEST) as the authoritative orchestration model. New cognitive actions must either map onto an existing lifecycle state or extend the lifecycle with a reviewed ADR.

alternatives.option: Use ad hoc booleans and per-feature execution flags
alternatives.rejected_because: This would fragment orchestration logic and make transition safety unverifiable.

alternatives.option: Collapse all non-awake behavior into a single background state
alternatives.rejected_because: This would erase important semantic differences between dreaming, normalization, adversarial scanning, and interactive lucid investigation.

expected: State transitions become a protected architectural seam
Tooling and docs can reason consistently about system behavior
New cognitive features must explicitly define how they enter and leave lifecycle states
risks: The lifecycle may feel heavyweight for experimental features
Adding new states requires deliberate governance

guard_rails: Do NOT add a new cognitive execution mode without mapping it to the lifecycle or recording a replacement ADR.
Do NOT bypass lifecycle transitions in tooling or extension integrations.
Do NOT merge lifecycle states solely for implementation convenience without reviewing downstream tool and prompt impacts.

decisions.title: Discipline sessions are mandatory governance for risky code modification workflows

context.problem: The repository includes a discipline subsystem, but there is no ADR documenting why modification tasks should be structured into evidence-backed phases with write protections.
constraints: The project is modified by humans and agents
Some tools can write source files and persistent knowledge
Ground-truth evidence is required before proposing or executing changes
Future contributors need clear expectations about when planning and verification are mandatory

decision.chosen: Use discipline sessions as the default governance mechanism for audits, ports, reconstructions, and non-trivial modifications. Evidence collection in INGEST/AUDIT, explicit planning, and post-change verification are the intended operating model for risky changes.

alternatives.option: Allow free-form modification without phase gating
alternatives.rejected_because: This increases the risk of unsupported claims, unsafe writes, and silent regressions.

alternatives.option: Use discipline only for external contributors
alternatives.rejected_because: Internal and agent-driven changes have the same need for traceable evidence and guarded execution.

expected: Safer write operations and better auditability
Improved reproducibility of agent-assisted changes
More explicit link between source-of-truth evidence and implemented diffs
risks: The workflow adds overhead for small changes
Tooling bugs in the discipline layer can block legitimate work

guard_rails: Do NOT weaken evidence requirements for risky code changes without a replacement governance mechanism.
Do NOT permit protected writes in modification workflows without an approved plan or equivalent explicit review policy.
Do NOT remove verification expectations for changes that alter behavior, persistence, or user-visible flows.

decisions.title: VS Code extension and backend communicate through an explicit, versioned contract

context.problem: The extension depends on backend/daemon behavior, but there is no ADR defining the trust boundary, failure handling expectations, or compatibility contract between the VS Code client and DreamGraph services.
constraints: The extension must remain usable when backend services are degraded or unavailable
Webview and extension-host state can diverge if contracts are implicit
The project may evolve backend APIs and extension UX independently

decision.chosen: Treat the VS Code extension ↔ backend interface as an explicit contract. Requests and responses should be versionable, capability-aware where needed, and designed for graceful degradation when the backend is unavailable.

alternatives.option: Rely on informal coupling between current extension code and server implementation
alternatives.rejected_because: This increases breakage risk and makes compatibility failures hard to diagnose.

alternatives.option: Push all state into the webview and use the extension host as a thin proxy
alternatives.rejected_because: This weakens host-side control over persistence, recovery, and instance-aware orchestration.

expected: Backend changes become easier to reason about and stage
The extension can implement clearer degraded/offline UX
State ownership remains concentrated in the extension host rather than fragmented in the webview
risks: Versioning introduces some protocol maintenance overhead
Capability mismatches need to be surfaced intentionally

guard_rails: Do NOT introduce breaking extension/backend message changes without a versioning or compatibility story.
Do NOT make the webview the sole source of truth for persistent chat or instance state.
Do NOT assume backend availability in user-facing extension flows without a degraded-mode response.

decisions.title: Chat conversation state in the VS Code extension is owned by the extension host and must survive webview recreation

context.problem: The chat UI can be torn down when users switch away and return, causing user-visible loss of conversation content if state depends on transient webview DOM state.
constraints: VS Code webviews may be hidden and recreated by the host
Users expect chat continuity within a workspace and instance
The extension already includes chat memory facilities and instance-aware behavior

decision.chosen: Keep the extension host as the authoritative owner of chat state and rehydrate any recreated or re-shown webview from host-held memory. Persist conversation history per DreamGraph instance so view switches and panel recreation do not erase the chat transcript.

alternatives.option: Store chat transcript only in the webview DOM or JavaScript runtime
alternatives.rejected_because: This state is lost when the webview is disposed or reloaded.

alternatives.option: Treat each chat panel reveal as a fresh session
alternatives.rejected_because: This breaks conversational continuity and frustrates users.

expected: Switching tabs/views will no longer erase the chat history
Extension-host logic remains the single source of truth for message history
Instance-aware chat restoration becomes deterministic
risks: Persisted history may need pruning or explicit clearing UX
Hydration logic must avoid duplicate rendering when panels are revived

guard_rails: Do NOT rely on transient webview memory as the only storage for chat transcript state.
Do NOT clear host-side chat state merely because the panel is hidden or recreated.
Do NOT add a second authoritative transcript store without defining reconciliation rules.

decisions.title: Runtime observability is a required companion to cognitive and extension behavior

context.problem: The system exposes many adaptive and stateful behaviors, but without runtime metrics it is difficult to validate tool reliability, cognitive strategy quality, or extension/backend failure patterns.
constraints: Observability should not block local development
Metrics should help explain behavior rather than merely count requests
The system includes both backend cognitive flows and UI client interactions

decision.chosen: Adopt runtime observability as a first-class operational requirement. Tool execution, cognitive transitions, schedule outcomes, and extension/backend failures should emit structured metrics or logs consumable by a configured runtime endpoint or local fallback sink.

alternatives.option: Rely only on static analysis and git history
alternatives.rejected_because: These cannot reveal production/runtime failure modes or usage patterns.

alternatives.option: Add telemetry only for backend HTTP requests
alternatives.rejected_because: This misses extension UX, cognitive scheduling, and internal tool behavior.

expected: Faster diagnosis of failure hotspots
Better calibration of cognitive strategies based on live evidence
Improved understanding of extension reliability and degraded modes
risks: Instrumentation adds implementation effort
Poorly scoped telemetry could create noise if not curated

guard_rails: Do NOT add major new cognitive or extension workflows without considering how they will be observed in runtime.
Do NOT treat absent runtime data as evidence that a feature is healthy.
Do NOT couple observability to a single external endpoint without a local fallback or graceful no-op mode.

decisions.title: Architect chat must use structured tool-calling rather than stream-only narration

context.problem: The VS Code architect chat panel delegated tool-capable requests to a placeholder that only streamed plain text. Because tool schemas were not sent to the provider API, the model narrated tool invocations as text/JSON instead of executing them, severing all MCP and local tool workflows.
constraints: The VS Code architect must support both MCP tools and local extension tools
Provider support must work across Anthropic and OpenAI-style tool-calling APIs
Tool execution state must be represented as iterative assistant tool_use and user tool_result turns
The extension must remain within the project workspace boundary and use existing local tool dispatch for filesystem and command execution

decision.chosen: Replace the stream-only placeholder path with a real iterative agentic loop that calls callWithTools, dispatches local or MCP tools based on the tool name, accumulates raw tool_use/tool_result messages, and continues until a non-tool final response is returned.

alternatives.option: Keep plain streaming and describe tools in prompt only
alternatives.rejected_because: This reproduces the failure mode where the model narrates intended actions without structured tool execution.

alternatives.option: Implement provider-specific tool loops directly in the chat panel without using architect-llm callWithTools
alternatives.rejected_because: This would duplicate logic already implemented in architect-llm and weaken cross-provider consistency.

expected: Architect responses can execute local and MCP tools instead of narrating them
File creation and other action-oriented tasks become achievable through the chat UI
Raw provider message translation remains centralized in architect-llm
Future tool failures can be debugged at the orchestration boundary with clearer provenance
risks: Iterative tool loops can create runaway execution if stop reasons are mishandled
Provider raw-message translation bugs can still cause partial failures
Tool result handling remains sensitive to malformed tool outputs

guard_rails: Do NOT route tool-capable architect requests through stream-only code paths.
Do NOT bypass architect-llm callWithTools when structured tool execution is required.
Do NOT replace iterative tool_use/tool_result accumulation with prompt-only descriptions of tool availability.

decisions.title: Preserve end-to-end agentic tool execution loop in VS Code chat panel

context.problem: The VS Code chat experience could narrate intended tool use without actually executing tools when the chat panel streamed placeholder text instead of running the architect LLM tool loop. This severed the end-to-end loop between model-emitted tool_use instructions and actual local/MCP tool execution, producing false success narratives and unreliable operational behavior.
constraints: All tool-capable chat responses must route through the architect LLM tool orchestration path rather than a placeholder streaming path.
The chat panel must preserve iterative execution semantics: model emits tool_use -> system executes tool -> tool_result is appended -> model continues until final answer.
Both MCP tools and local support tools are part of the supported execution surface and must remain invocable from the same loop.
User-visible success claims must be grounded in actual executed tool results, not inferred intent or narrated plans.
Changes must stay within the VS Code extension project boundary and avoid direct mutation of protected graph data outside approved MCP tools.

decision.chosen: The VS Code chat panel must use the architect LLM's tool-capable call path as the authoritative execution mechanism for chat interactions that may invoke tools. The system must maintain a closed-loop agentic workflow: gather tool definitions, invoke callWithTools, detect tool_use outputs, dispatch each tool call to the appropriate executor (local support tool or MCP tool), append structured tool_result messages, and continue iterating until the model returns a final answer without pending tool calls.

alternatives.option: Keep placeholder stream()-based chat rendering and treat tool mentions as informational only
alternatives.rejected_because: This creates a misleading user experience where the assistant appears to act without executing tools, breaking trust and preventing real orchestration.

alternatives.option: Allow separate ad hoc execution paths for local tools and MCP tools
alternatives.rejected_because: Multiple execution paths increase drift risk, make verification harder, and can break the required tool_result continuation semantics.

alternatives.option: Rely on manual operator verification instead of enforcing execution-loop integrity in code
alternatives.rejected_because: Manual verification can catch regressions after the fact but does not prevent false success claims or broken automation at runtime.

expected: Chat responses that mention tool activity will be backed by actual tool executions.
The architect LLM layer remains the single authoritative translation point for provider-specific tool-call formats.
Future regressions are easier to detect because the execution chain is conceptually explicit: tool_use -> execute -> tool_result -> continue.
The extension can safely support mixed local and MCP orchestration in one conversation loop.
risks: The iterative tool loop is more complex than a plain streaming response path and may regress if refactored without preserving stop-reason handling.
Provider-specific response-shape changes could break tool_use detection unless translation remains maintained.
Error handling or rate-limit behavior may still cause partial executions if not surfaced clearly to the user.

guard_rails: Do NOT replace the chat panel's tool-capable execution path with a placeholder or display-only streaming path for interactions that may invoke tools.
Do NOT claim that a tool action succeeded unless a corresponding tool execution result was actually received and incorporated into the conversation.
Do NOT split local-tool and MCP-tool orchestration into incompatible loops that bypass the shared tool_result continuation mechanism.
Do NOT modify architect tool-call translation behavior without validating that emitted tool_use events still reach the chat-panel execution loop end-to-end.

decisions.title: Use repository engine.env template for new instance creation with programmatic fallback

context.problem: New DreamGraph instances currently generate config/engine.env programmatically inside instance lifecycle code, while a repository template also exists under templates/default/config. This duplicates configuration defaults, risks drift when new environment variables are introduced, and makes onboarding documentation harder to keep correct. Instance creation should prefer a human-maintained default template when available, while remaining robust if the template is missing.
constraints: New instance creation must continue to succeed even if the repository template is unavailable.
The default engine.env must live in the repository templates/default/config directory and may also be mirrored into the global ~/.dreamgraph/templates/default/config directory.
New engine.env variables should be represented in the default template as commented-out entries so users can discover all configurable options.
Per-instance config/engine.env remains an override layer loaded by src/utils/engine-env.ts at startup.
Changes must stay within the current instance lifecycle architecture and not break existing dg init behavior.

decision.chosen: When creating a new instance, DreamGraph must first attempt to copy config/engine.env from the repository template path templates/default/config/engine.env (and future compatible template locations if introduced). If no template file is available, it must fall back to generating engine.env programmatically as it does today. The repository template becomes the primary source of truth for the default commented-out engine.env content. Future introduction of new engine environment variables must include updating this default template so newly created instances expose them discoverably.

alternatives.option: Keep generating engine.env only in code
alternatives.rejected_because: This duplicates defaults, hides available variables from maintainers, and causes documentation and onboarding drift when new variables are added.

alternatives.option: Require template presence and fail instance creation if missing
alternatives.rejected_because: This would make dg init brittle and regress current reliability guarantees.

alternatives.option: Use only a global ~/.dreamgraph template outside the repository
alternatives.rejected_because: Repository-controlled defaults are needed for versioned source-of-truth behavior and contributor visibility.

expected: New instances will inherit a single maintained default engine.env template when available.
Instance creation remains reliable because programmatic fallback still works.
Adding new engine env variables will require template maintenance as part of the change.
Documentation and generated defaults will stay easier to align with actual onboarding behavior.
risks: Template and fallback code may still drift if maintainers forget to update both when new variables are introduced.
Multiple template locations could become inconsistent if not intentionally synchronized.

guard_rails: Do NOT remove the programmatic engine.env fallback unless template availability is guaranteed and migration is planned.
Do NOT introduce new engine environment variables without updating the default engine.env template content to include them as commented-out examples.
Do NOT change new-instance engine.env creation behavior to depend exclusively on user-specific global template files.

decisions.title: Support named global instance templates for dg init

context.problem: New instances need a clear, reusable template mechanism so users can prepare multiple instance configuration presets under ~/.dreamgraph/templates and select one during dg init. Without an explicit architectural rule, template resolution and documentation can drift, and dg init help/docs may under-specify how template selection works.
constraints: Must stay within the ~/.dreamgraph master directory boundary
Must preserve programmatic fallback when no named template exists
Must remain compatible with existing default template-first instance creation behavior from ADR-008
Users, not the repo, are responsible for creating additional named templates such as openai or anthropic

decision.chosen: dg init supports --template <name> with default 'default'. Instance creation resolves templates in this order: ~/.dreamgraph/templates/<name> first, repository templates/<name> second, built-in programmatic scaffold last. Install scripts copy the repository templates/default tree into the global templates area and overwrite only with force or explicit user confirmation. Documentation and command help must describe that users can create additional templates by copying and renaming ~/.dreamgraph/templates/default.

alternatives.option: Support only a hardcoded default template
alternatives.rejected_because: Prevents user-managed presets and does not meet the requirement for reusable named templates such as openai.

alternatives.option: Require all templates to live only in the repository
alternatives.rejected_because: Makes per-user reusable presets awkward and undermines the purpose of ~/.dreamgraph/templates.

alternatives.option: Remove programmatic fallback and require a template always exist
alternatives.rejected_because: Reduces robustness and conflicts with ADR-008 resilience requirements.

expected: Users can prepare multiple reusable instance presets under ~/.dreamgraph/templates
dg init help and docs become explicit about template selection and customization
Default installation behavior keeps the global default template aligned with the repository template unless the user preserves a custom installation
risks: Template content may drift if new environment variables are added and templates are not updated
User-customized templates may be overwritten if force/overwrite is used intentionally

guard_rails: Do NOT remove the fallback chain: global template -> repository template -> programmatic scaffold without replacing it with an equally robust mechanism.
Do NOT make dg init template selection implicit or undocumented; --template behavior must remain discoverable via dg init --help and setup docs.
Do NOT assume named templates exist in the repository beyond default; users must be able to create them in ~/.dreamgraph/templates.

decisions.title: Canonical Feature Identity Uses feature_* IDs

context.problem: The fact graph contains duplicate and legacy feature identities for the same architectural areas, especially dashboard and VS Code extension surfaces (for example feature_dashboard_server vs dashboard/dashboard_server and feature_vscode_extension vs vscode_extension/extensions_vscode). This fragments ownership, weakens UI registry used_by mappings, and makes graph queries ambiguous.
constraints: Must preserve existing graph data without destructive deletion
UI registry ownership should resolve to stable feature IDs
Changes must remain within existing DreamGraph feature/data protection model
No accepted ADR currently defines canonical naming for feature identities

decision.chosen: Use feature_* IDs as the canonical identity scheme for authoritative feature entities. Legacy non-canonical feature entries may remain temporarily for historical continuity, but all new enrichment and UI registry used_by mappings must target canonical feature_* IDs. Consolidation work should strengthen canonical entries and mark legacy aliases as superseded in descriptions/metadata rather than relying on them for ownership.

alternatives.option: Keep mixed historical IDs indefinitely
alternatives.rejected_because: Leaves graph queries ambiguous and preserves fragmented ownership semantics.

alternatives.option: Delete legacy feature entries immediately
alternatives.rejected_because: Higher risk because other graph references may still point at those IDs and DreamGraph lacks a dedicated feature-delete/supersede flow.

alternatives.option: Use source-path-derived IDs as canonical feature identifiers
alternatives.rejected_because: Would be less stable for conceptual features spanning multiple files and UIs.

expected: UI registry ownership becomes consistent across dashboard and extension surfaces
Future enrichment converges on stable canonical feature identifiers
Legacy aliases can still be discovered during transition but should no longer own semantics
risks: Some existing queries may still return legacy features until broader cleanup is complete
Without a dedicated deprecation mechanism for features, legacy nodes remain visible and may confuse users temporarily

guard_rails: Do NOT introduce new authoritative feature entities for existing capabilities unless they follow the feature_* canonical ID scheme.
Do NOT register UI used_by ownership against legacy aliases when a canonical feature_* entity already exists.
Do NOT treat dashboard, dashboard_server, server_dashboard, vscode_extension, or extensions_vscode as authoritative owners while canonical feature_* entries exist.

decisions.title: Semantic UI Registry Includes Abstract Visual Language and Layout Contracts

context.problem: The current semantic UI registry captures purpose, data contracts, interactions, implementations, and ownership, but it under-specifies visual styling and layout characteristics that are architecturally important for preserving consistent UX across dashboard and extension surfaces. Without abstract visual metadata, the registry cannot fully describe composition intent, emphasis hierarchy, spacing density, navigation chrome, or state-driven styling while remaining platform-agnostic.
constraints: UI registry must remain semantic and platform-agnostic rather than storing raw CSS or framework-specific style props.
Visual metadata must describe intent and layout contracts, not pixel-perfect implementation details.
Existing registered UI elements should remain valid and be enrichable incrementally.
Metadata should support both server-rendered dashboard HTML and VS Code extension surfaces.

decision.chosen: Extend the semantic UI registry convention to include abstract visual and layout metadata for UI elements. This metadata should describe visual role, density, emphasis, chrome level, layout pattern, alignment, hierarchy, responsive behavior, and state-driven styling semantics, while avoiding concrete CSS values or implementation-specific component props.

alternatives.option: Keep registry purely behavioral and omit visual/layout metadata
alternatives.rejected_because: Leaves an architectural blind spot where shared UX structure and visual intent are undocumented and hard to port or validate.

alternatives.option: Store raw CSS/design-token/framework style props directly in the registry
alternatives.rejected_because: Violates platform abstraction and would couple the registry to specific implementations rather than semantic intent.

expected: UI registry entries can better express cross-platform UX intent and composition rules.
Migration and reconstruction tasks can preserve layout and visual hierarchy more accurately.
Some existing UI elements will need incremental enrichment to adopt the expanded metadata model.
risks: Visual metadata may drift toward implementation detail if not governed carefully.
Different contributors may interpret abstract styling categories inconsistently until conventions stabilize.

guard_rails: Do NOT store raw CSS, Tailwind classes, or framework-specific style props as authoritative UI registry metadata.
Do NOT replace semantic purpose/data-contract metadata with purely visual descriptions; visual metadata is additive.

When registering or updating UI elements, prefer abstract layout and visual intent terms such as card grid, dense inspector, primary action emphasis, or embedded shell chrome over pixel-level specifications.

decisions.title: UI Registry Supports Abstract Visual and Layout Semantics With Backward Compatibility

context.problem: The semantic UI registry captured purpose, data contracts, and interactions, but lacked first-class fields for abstract visual language and layout contracts. This limited reconstruction, migration planning, and design reasoning. The system needed these semantics without breaking existing registry entries or callers.
constraints: Must preserve backward compatibility for existing ui_registry.json entries and existing register_ui_element callers
Must keep the registry abstract and platform-independent
Must not store raw CSS classes, Tailwind utilities, pixel spacing, or framework-specific style props as authoritative registry data
Must continue supporting existing migration and query tools

decision.chosen: Extend the SemanticElement and register_ui_element schema with optional visual_semantics and layout_semantics fields, treat them as non-breaking enrichment, and bump the UI registry schema metadata to 1.1.0 while keeping older entries readable.

alternatives.option: Keep encoding visual/layout intent only in tags and notes
alternatives.rejected_because: Too weakly structured for reliable querying, migration planning, and architectural validation

alternatives.option: Store raw implementation styling details in the registry
alternatives.rejected_because: Violates abstraction boundaries and would couple the registry to specific UI stacks

expected: UI elements can now carry first-class abstract visual and layout metadata
Existing registry entries remain valid without migration
Future UI reasoning and migration planning can use stronger semantics
risks: Some existing consumers may ignore the new fields until updated
Abstract semantics may be modeled inconsistently unless governed by ADR guard rails

guard_rails: Do NOT require visual_semantics or layout_semantics for legacy UI entries to remain valid
Do NOT store raw CSS classes, framework utility tokens, or pixel values in the UI registry as authoritative metadata
Do NOT break existing register_ui_element payloads that omit the new fields

decisions.title: Canonical UI Registry Uses Semantic ui_* IDs and Transitional Legacy Entries

context.problem: The UI registry contains overlapping legacy and canonical entries for similar dashboard and extension surfaces, which causes exported docs and graph queries to mix authoritative semantic elements with older aliases or parallel representations.
constraints: Preserve backward compatibility for existing registry consumers and older references.
Do not delete legacy entries without a dedicated retirement mechanism.
Canonical entries must remain abstract and platform-independent.
Registry ownership should align with ADR-010 feature identity conventions.

decision.chosen: Treat semantically named ui_* entries and the established canonical dashboard/extension surfaces as authoritative. Legacy or parallel UI entries remain transitional references only and must not be preferred in new ownership mappings, new docs examples, or future enrichment passes.

alternatives.option: Delete duplicate legacy UI entries immediately
alternatives.rejected_because: There is no dedicated non-destructive retirement flow for UI elements, and immediate deletion risks breaking historical references.

alternatives.option: Keep enriching all legacy and canonical entries equally
alternatives.rejected_because: That would preserve ambiguity and continue to pollute the registry with overlapping authoritative representations.

expected: Future registry enrichment will target canonical ui_* entries first.
Exported docs can be interpreted with a clear distinction between canonical and transitional UI entities.
Ownership mappings and examples become more consistent across dashboard and extension surfaces.
risks: Legacy duplicate UI entries still remain queryable until a retirement mechanism exists.
Some consumers may still surface legacy entries unless additional filtering is added in docs or queries.

guard_rails: Do NOT create new authoritative UI registry entries for existing surfaces when a canonical ui_* entry already exists.
Do NOT prefer legacy or parallel non-canonical UI entries in used_by mappings, examples, or enrichment passes when a canonical entry exists.
Do NOT encode platform-specific styling tokens into canonical UI registry entries.

decisions.title: UI Registry Supports Backward-Compatible Retirement and Export Filtering

context.problem: The UI registry contained canonical ui_* entries alongside legacy or parallel entries. Without lifecycle metadata, exports and queries surfaced all entries equally, making the semantic inventory noisy and making canonicalization incomplete.
constraints: Must remain backward compatible with existing ui_registry.json data and register_ui_element payloads.
Must not delete historical UI entries destructively.
Canonical ui_* entries established by ADR-013 must remain authoritative.
Living docs should prefer active canonical entries while still preserving historical traceability.

decision.chosen: Add optional UI registry lifecycle fields (status, superseded_by, deprecation_reason). Treat omitted status as active for backward compatibility. Extend query/export behavior so deprecated entries can be filtered from primary views while still being documented as legacy references.

alternatives.option: Delete legacy UI entries outright
alternatives.rejected_because: Would lose historical traceability and risks breaking existing references.

alternatives.option: Keep legacy entries without lifecycle metadata
alternatives.rejected_because: Leaves canonicalization ambiguous and docs noisy.

expected: Canonical UI entries become easier to identify in queries and exports.
Legacy entries remain available for compatibility but no longer dominate primary documentation.
Future retirement of overlapping UI entries can be done non-destructively.
risks: Some existing exports may show newly added deprecated sections, changing documentation shape slightly.
Legacy entries without explicit superseded_by values would remain ambiguous until curated.

guard_rails: Do NOT require lifecycle fields on older UI registry entries; omitted status must continue to mean active.
Do NOT delete legacy UI entries when a non-destructive deprecated or transitional state is sufficient.
Do NOT include deprecated UI entries in primary migration planning by default.
Do NOT let deprecated legacy entries outrank canonical ui_* entries in exported documentation.

decisions.title: API Security Layer Implementation

context.problem: To ensure secure interactions with the API, preventing unauthorized access and data breaches.
constraints: All API requests must be authenticated
Sensitive data must be encrypted in transit

decision.chosen: Implement an API Security Layer that enforces authentication and encryption.

alternatives.option: No security layer
alternatives.rejected_because: Increased risk of unauthorized access and data breaches.

alternatives.option: Basic token authentication
alternatives.rejected_because: Insufficient for protecting sensitive data.

expected: Improved security posture for API interactions.
risks: Potential performance overhead due to security checks.

guard_rails: Do NOT change security protocols without reviewing this ADR.

decisions.title: Data Storage Strategy

context.problem: To ensure efficient and reliable data management across the application.
constraints: Transactional data must be stored in a relational database
Configuration data must be stored in JSON files

decision.chosen: Use a relational database for transactional data and JSON files for configuration.

alternatives.option: Store all data in a NoSQL database
alternatives.rejected_because: Does not meet transactional consistency requirements.

alternatives.option: Use XML for configuration
alternatives.rejected_because: JSON is more lightweight and easier to parse.

expected: Improved data integrity and easier configuration management.
risks: Migration challenges if data storage strategy changes in the future.

guard_rails: Do NOT change data storage formats without reviewing this ADR.

decisions.title: Integration Pattern for External Services

context.problem: To enable seamless communication with external services while maintaining system integrity.
constraints: All external integrations must use webhooks for asynchronous communication

decision.chosen: Implement webhook-based integrations for external services.

alternatives.option: Polling for external service updates
alternatives.rejected_because: Inefficient and increases latency.

alternatives.option: Direct API calls
alternatives.rejected_because: Tight coupling with external services.

expected: Reduced latency and improved responsiveness to external events.
risks: Webhook failures could lead to missed events.

guard_rails: Do NOT change integration patterns without reviewing this ADR.

decisions.title: Cognitive Engine Architecture

context.problem: To manage cognitive reasoning and decision-making processes effectively.
constraints: Cognitive engine must support modular components for flexibility

decision.chosen: Adopt a modular architecture for the cognitive engine.
