atomicWriteFile must default to UTF-8 so callers do not have to repeat the encoding flag
Failure path must clean up the orphan .tmp where possible without masking the original error

decision.chosen: All persistent JSON state writes go through src/utils/atomic-write.ts (open \u2192 writeFile \u2192 fdatasync \u2192 close \u2192 rename) for the async path. The synchronous engine-env initializer in src/utils/engine-env.ts mirrors the same pattern with openSync \u2192 writeFileSync \u2192 fdatasyncSync \u2192 closeSync \u2192 renameSync, and unlinks the orphan .tmp on failure. Audit pass converted 8 sites: attach.ts (3), export.ts (3), fork.ts (1), engine-env.ts (1).

expected: Crash or power loss during a write leaves the original file intact and at most a harmless orphan .tmp
Operators can trust that data/*.json files are either the prior valid version or the new valid version, never a partial truncation
New code adding a writeFile against persistent state is an obvious code-smell visible in review
risks: Inline sync atomic pattern in engine-env.ts duplicates the helper's logic and can drift
The orphan .tmp cleanup is best-effort; if both rename and unlink fail, the .tmp lingers (harmless but noisy)
Atomic rename is per-filesystem; cross-device renames will fail (mitigated: temp file is in same directory as target)

guard_rails: Do NOT add a raw writeFile() / writeFileSync() against any data/*.json or instance.json path — always go through atomicWriteFile or its sync mirror
Do NOT skip fdatasync; rename without fdatasync can still expose torn writes on some filesystems
Do NOT swallow rename errors silently — propagate so the caller knows the write was not durable
When adding new sync write sites, replicate the engine-env.ts inline pattern rather than blocking on the async helper

decisions.title: LLM request timeout is a configurable LlmConfig field driven by env var

context.problem: All LLM provider implementations had hardcoded request timeouts. Operators running larger local models that legitimately exceeded the default could not extend the budget without editing source. There was no environment-variable knob and no shared LlmConfig field for the timeout.
constraints: Default behaviour must be preserved (120 s budget) for operators who do not set the env var
All four provider constructors must accept the new parameter with a default value (backward source-compat)
Liveness probes stay short-circuited; only the completion path honours the configured timeout
The dashboard.ts LlmConfig literal must include timeoutMs so TypeScript stays clean

decision.chosen: Add LlmConfig.timeoutMs (number, ms). parseLlmConfig() reads DREAMGRAPH_LLM_TIMEOUT_MS from env and defaults to 120_000 ms when unset or invalid. initLlmProvider() threads c.timeoutMs into all four provider constructors (ollama, openai, lmstudio, anthropic). Each provider stores it as a private field and uses AbortSignal.timeout(this.timeoutMs) on the actual completion fetch. Liveness probes (3 s ollama / 5 s openai-compatible) intentionally retain hardcoded short timeouts \u2014 they test reachability, not request budget.

expected: Operators running large local models (e.g. 70B+) can extend the LLM request budget without code edits
Default behaviour is unchanged; existing deployments need no migration
Dashboard, scheduler, and dream cycle paths all share the same configurable timeout
risks: Setting the env var to an unreasonably large value (e.g. hours) can mask a hung provider; operators must choose responsibly
The cap is per request, not per session — a stuck provider can still consume budget across many calls
Negative or zero values fall back to the 120_000 default; this is intentional but may surprise operators expecting an instant-fail mode

guard_rails: Do NOT hardcode timeouts in provider implementations — always accept timeoutMs and use AbortSignal.timeout(this.timeoutMs)
Do NOT change the liveness-probe short timeouts to use the configured value; reachability and request-budget are different concerns
If adding a new provider, accept timeoutMs as the last constructor parameter with default 120_000 to match existing providers
The default (120_000) and the env var name (DREAMGRAPH_LLM_TIMEOUT_MS) are part of the operator contract — do not rename without a migration note

decisions.title: DreamGraph success pattern: Hypothesis → Restraint → Pressure → Resolution → Validation

context.problem: Recurring weak-connection tension can indicate a real architectural relationship before the graph has admissible proof. The system needs a reusable pattern describing when repeated resurfacing is healthy rather than pathological.
constraints: Validated graph edges remain the threshold for proven fact.
Recurring tension alone must not be promoted to truth without admissible structural evidence.
Low resurfacing rate is acceptable when it preserves epistemic restraint.
Dream-cycle linking may supply missing intermediate structure over time.

decision.chosen: Treat the sequence Hypothesis → Restraint → Pressure → Resolution → Validation as a positive DreamGraph success pattern when a repeatedly resurfacing tension remains unproven until later dream-cycle or graph-linking work produces a validated semantic path. In this pattern, repeated pressure is interpreted as healthy persistence of uncertainty, not failure, provided the system continues to withhold truth claims until validated edges exist.

alternatives.option: Suppress recurring tensions earlier to reduce repeated resurfacing
alternatives.rejected_because: This would reduce pressure on unresolved but meaningful hypotheses and could hide real but not-yet-provable relationships.

alternatives.option: Promote recurring weak connections to fact after enough repetitions
alternatives.rejected_because: This would weaken epistemic discipline and risk converting strong intuition into unsupported truth claims.

expected: DreamGraph narratives can distinguish healthy repeated hypothesis pressure from faulty churn.
Operators have a named reference pattern for interpreting low-rate recurring tensions that later validate.
Future design discussions can point to this pattern when evaluating dream-cycle value and tension suppression policy.
risks: Operators may overuse the pattern to justify tensions that never validate.
A named success pattern could be misread as endorsing all resurfacing rather than only restrained, eventually validated cases.

guard_rails: Do NOT treat recurrence count alone as proof; validated semantic graph evidence remains required.
Do NOT classify resurfacing as a success pattern unless the relationship later resolves through explicit validated structure.
Do NOT use this pattern to bypass investigation of genuinely noisy or pathological tension generators.

decisions.title: Retarget API workflow weak-connection analysis to the specific API workflow node

context.problem: A recurring weak-connection pattern used the generic workflow entity as the target for dreamgraph_src_api_routes, which blurred a concrete API orchestration workflow that now exists in the graph.
constraints: Accepted graph facts should prefer the most specific validated or intentionally curated workflow node available.
Generic abstraction targets should not hide concrete workflow structure when a specific workflow is architecturally real.
Analytics interpretation should distinguish workflow model links from concrete API workflow links.

decision.chosen: Future interpretation of the API-routes-to-workflow weak-connection case should target workflow_api_graph_context_loop instead of the generic workflow entity when discussing convergence, analytics, and remediation.

alternatives.option: Keep using the generic workflow entity as the primary target
alternatives.rejected_because: It preserves the broad conceptual link but loses the concrete API workflow semantics now present in the graph.

expected: Recurring analytics around this case become more specific and easier to interpret.
Future convergence analysis can distinguish conceptual workflow-model linkage from concrete API workflow linkage.
DreamGraph architecture memory preserves the intended target refinement even before all tensions are re-derived.
risks: If a different API workflow later proves more appropriate, this targeting guidance may need revision.
This records interpretation guidance; existing historical tension rows may still reference the older generic target.

guard_rails: Do NOT treat the generic workflow entity as the preferred target for this API-routes case when a specific API workflow node exists.
Do NOT claim historical tension rows were automatically rewritten; this ADR changes interpretation guidance, not past log records.

decisions.title: Tool naming must carry primary semantics so tool descriptions need not be injected into model context

context.problem: Tool descriptions consume prompt budget and create dependency on out-of-band prose for basic tool use. In the SDK and extension tool surfaces, models should be able to infer a tool's purpose primarily from the tool name and parameter names/signatures. If a tool's behavior is not reasonably inferable from name(params) alone, that indicates poor naming or over-broad responsibility.
constraints: Tool names must remain concise enough for provider tool schemas and logs.
Parameter names must be semantically meaningful and disambiguate scope, target, and side effects.
Existing tools may need compatibility shims or aliases to avoid breaking callers immediately.
Some edge cases still require machine-readable schema constraints, but not explanatory prose for primary intent.
Naming should work across providers and SDK surfaces without relying on provider-specific prompt stuffing.

decision.chosen: Adopt an ADR guard rail that tool interfaces are self-describing by name and parameters. Do not rely on injected natural-language tool descriptions as the primary mechanism for tool understanding. When designing or revising a tool, require that an informed reader can infer the main behavior from toolName(paramNames) alone. Treat failure of that test as a design smell that should trigger renaming, decomposition, or narrower parameterization before adding descriptive context.

alternatives.option: Continue passing rich tool descriptions in prompt context
alternatives.rejected_because: Consumes context budget, duplicates schema intent in prose, and hides weak naming behind prompt engineering.

alternatives.option: Keep current names but add more examples/documentation in prompts
alternatives.rejected_because: Improves one runtime path only and does not fix the underlying interface clarity problem.

alternatives.option: Use opaque stable IDs for tools and depend entirely on external registry metadata
alternatives.rejected_because: Maximizes indirection and makes ad hoc model reasoning and human inspection worse.

expected: Reduced prompt/context overhead for tool calling.
Stronger pressure toward smaller, more precise tool interfaces.
Easier cross-provider portability because the interface semantics live in the schema surface.
Some existing tool names may be identified as needing rename or split work.
Documentation remains useful for edge cases, constraints, and examples, but not for conveying the tool's basic purpose.
risks: Renaming tools can break existing callers if migration is not staged.
Over-indexing on brevity may produce names that are concise but still ambiguous.
A few legitimate complex tools may resist full semantic compression into name(params) alone.

guard_rails: Before introducing a new tool, apply the self-describing test: can the primary behavior be inferred from toolName(paramNames) without extra prose?
If not, prefer renaming the tool, renaming parameters, or splitting the tool into narrower operations before adding description text.
Use descriptions for edge behavior, constraints, caveats, and examples—not as the only place the tool's main action is explained.
Avoid umbrella tool names that conceal multiple unrelated behaviors behind generic parameters.
When compatibility requires retaining a poor legacy name, add a clearly named alias and deprecate the ambiguous surface.

decisions.title: Adaptive Result Delivery Uses Targets, Expectations, and Explicit Compromise Instead of Hard Limits

context.problem: DreamGraph tool and transport responses can vary in size and fidelity across producer, serialization, transport, client, and history layers. Modeling these behaviors as fixed hard result limits leads to incorrect reasoning, misleading diagnostics, and brittle implementation choices. For this kind of cognitive system, hard-size enforcement is a poor fit because it hides partial success and prevents adaptive recovery strategies.
constraints: The system operates across multiple layers where payload degradation may occur after successful tool execution.
Response sizing behavior is soft and context-dependent rather than governed by a single authoritative constant.
The system must support progressive narrowing and recovery when large responses are difficult to deliver intact.
Existing tooling and callers may need backward-compatible response evolution rather than abrupt clipping or hard failure semantics.

decision.chosen: DreamGraph will not model response delivery through fixed hard result limits as the primary policy. Instead, it will use adaptive targets and expectations for result delivery, and when ideal delivery cannot be preserved it should favor explicit compromise signaling and recovery guidance over hard-cap language or premature clipping.

alternatives.option: Keep or introduce fixed hard result limits
alternatives.rejected_because: This creates false certainty, encourages brittle behavior, conflates producer success with downstream delivery loss, and is a poor fit for adaptive cognitive tooling.

alternatives.option: Silently clip oversized results without signaling
alternatives.rejected_because: This destroys context, obscures failure modes, and prevents callers from recovering intelligently.

alternatives.option: Treat truncation as purely a client concern with no architectural guidance
alternatives.rejected_because: This leaves the system without a shared reasoning model and leads to inconsistent diagnostics and response-shaping decisions.

expected: Diagnostics will shift from hard-cap language toward target/expectation/compromise language.
Tool and transport behavior can evolve adaptively without violating an artificial constant-limit model.
Large-response handling should increasingly provide recovery hints and navigable structure rather than relying on clipping.
Agents and humans will be better able to distinguish producer success from downstream compromise.
risks: Without careful wording, adaptive behavior may become too vague for implementers.
Different subsystems may interpret targets and compromises inconsistently.
Some callers may still assume hard ceilings and require migration in language or expectations.

guard_rails: Do not describe result delivery as governed by a single hard constant unless code and runtime policy explicitly prove that is true.
Prefer additive response metadata and explicit compromise signaling over silent clipping.
When large payload delivery degrades, preserve or expose recovery paths such as narrowing, sub-entity targeting, or structured summaries.
Distinguish tool execution success from downstream delivery fidelity in diagnostics and user-facing reasoning.

decisions.title: Canonical M1 runtime metrics snapshot aligns /metrics, system://metrics, and query_runtime_metrics

context.problem: Runtime observability surfaces were diverging: internal metrics sources existed, but the canonical contract for M1 runtime observability was not uniformly represented across the shared adapter, HTTP endpoint, resource surface, and tool surface. Without a single snapshot schema, future consumers could drift and produce incompatible metrics payloads.
constraints: Preserve graceful behavior when runtime metrics are disabled or no external endpoint is configured.
Use the existing shared consolidation point in src/observability/runtime-metrics.ts rather than creating parallel metrics adapters.
Keep the initial M1 schema operationally useful even if some buckets are derived heuristically from current tool and graph metrics sources.
Allow local/private HTTP exposure for /metrics in M1 without requiring public deployment hardening.
Align resource and tool surfaces to the same canonical snapshot semantics wherever feasible.

decision.chosen: Adopt src/observability/runtime-metrics.ts as the canonical producer of RuntimeMetricsSnapshotV1 using the nested M1 schema. The HTTP /metrics endpoint, the system://metrics resource, and the query_runtime_metrics tool should all align to this canonical snapshot model. In M1, /metrics is gated by an explicit enable flag and restricted to local/private use, while resource/tool surfaces may use the same snapshot directly or via configured endpoint retrieval depending on context.

alternatives.option: Let each surface (/metrics, resources, tools) shape its own metrics payload independently
alternatives.rejected_because: This would reintroduce contract drift and make observability consumers unreliable.

alternatives.option: Keep the previous flat metrics schema until all downstream consumers are implemented
alternatives.rejected_because: The flat schema does not match the approved M1 plan and would force later breaking changes across more consumers.

alternatives.option: Expose only an external endpoint-backed query_runtime_metrics tool and avoid internal canonicalization
alternatives.rejected_because: This would make local validation harder and leave resource/HTTP surfaces semantically inconsistent.

expected: Runtime observability consumers have a single M1 snapshot contract to target.
Future additions to metrics buckets can be made in one shared adapter and flow to HTTP/resource/tool surfaces consistently.
There is a clear implementation anchor for M1 observability alignment across runtime surfaces.
risks: Some current bucket derivations are heuristic because existing low-level metrics sources were not originally designed around the exact M1 schema.
Consumers not yet migrated may still assume the previous flat shape.
Async/sync signature changes in the canonical snapshot producer may require follow-up alignment if hidden call sites exist.

guard_rails: Do NOT introduce a second canonical runtime metrics adapter while RuntimeMetricsSnapshotV1 is owned by src/observability/runtime-metrics.ts.
Do NOT let /metrics, system://metrics, or query_runtime_metrics drift to incompatible payload schemas without explicitly revisiting this decision.
Do NOT expose /metrics broadly by default in M1; keep it explicitly enabled and locally constrained unless a later decision hardens it for wider deployment.
Do NOT treat absent or partial runtime data as evidence of feature health; observability gaps remain possible.

decisions.title: SDK webhooks are core service first and plugin-consumable later

context.problem: The SDK roadmap needed to decide whether webhooks should be implemented as plugin-provided functionality or as a core DreamGraph service before plugins consume webhook capabilities.
constraints: Webhook delivery touches secrets, signing, retries, dead-letter queues, replay, and operator trust.
Plugin code must not receive broad authority over delivery security or operational reliability by default.
The plugin SDK should expose stable consumable capabilities only after the core service defines the trust and operational model.
related_tensions: core platform responsibility vs plugin flexibility

decision.chosen: Implement webhook delivery as a core service first. Make it plugin-consumable later through host-mediated capabilities once delivery, signing, retry, DLQ, replay, and audit semantics are mature.

alternatives.option: Let plugins implement webhook delivery directly in MVP
alternatives.rejected_because: Would delegate secrets, signing, retries, replay, and failure handling to arbitrary plugins before the trust model is established.

alternatives.option: Exclude webhooks entirely from the plugin roadmap
alternatives.rejected_because: Plugins are expected to benefit from webhook events later, but they should consume a core service rather than own delivery.

expected: Core owns webhook security and delivery semantics.
Plugins can later subscribe to or emit webhook-relevant events through a constrained host-mediated API.
The MVP plugin surface remains smaller and safer.
risks: Core webhook implementation may become a bottleneck for plugin-driven integrations.
The later plugin-consumable API must avoid leaking secrets or replay authority.

guard_rails: Do not grant plugins arbitrary webhook delivery authority before the core webhook service exists.
Do not store signing secrets or retry/DLQ policy inside untrusted plugin packages.
Do not expose webhook replay or delivery mutation operations to plugins without explicit host-mediated authorization.

decisions.title: Plugin management is bundled into the existing dg CLI

context.problem: The SDK roadmap needed to decide whether plugin management should use a separate toolchain or become part of the existing DreamGraph command-line interface.
constraints: Plugin management is instance administration.
Operators should not need a separate plugin-specific CLI toolchain for normal administration.
The existing dg CLI is the natural administrative surface for DreamGraph instances.
related_tensions: single administrative surface vs separate plugin toolchain

decision.chosen: Bundle plugin management commands into the existing dg CLI under dg plugin rather than creating a separate CLI.

alternatives.option: Create a standalone plugin CLI
alternatives.rejected_because: Would split instance administration across multiple tools and increase operator burden.

alternatives.option: Leave plugin management entirely manual
alternatives.rejected_because: Would undermine repeatable installation, inspection, enabling, disabling, and lifecycle management.

expected: Operators administer plugins through the same dg tool used for the rest of DreamGraph.
Documentation and automation can standardize on dg plugin commands.
Future plugin lifecycle commands should fit under the existing CLI command hierarchy.
risks: The dg CLI can become crowded if plugin commands are not organized carefully.
CLI implementation must preserve clear separation between plugin administration and runtime plugin authority.

guard_rails: Do not introduce a separate first-party plugin management CLI without superseding this decision.
Keep plugin lifecycle administration under dg plugin or a clearly compatible dg subcommand hierarchy.
Do not let CLI convenience bypass plugin trust, signing, allowlist, or capability checks.

decisions.title: DreamGraph plugin packages use the dreamgraph-plugin-* naming convention

context.problem: The SDK roadmap needed a stable naming convention for plugin discovery, marketplace indexing, and ecosystem expectations.
constraints: Plugin packages need recognizable naming for discovery and review.
The convention should be simple enough for package registries and documentation.
A stable prefix helps separate DreamGraph plugins from unrelated packages.
related_tensions: ecosystem consistency vs package author flexibility

decision.chosen: Lock in dreamgraph-plugin-* as the package naming convention for DreamGraph plugins.

alternatives.option: Use @dreamgraph/plugin-* only
alternatives.rejected_because: A scoped-only convention may not fit all registries or community package ownership patterns.

alternatives.option: Allow arbitrary package names with manifest metadata only
alternatives.rejected_because: Would make discovery, review, and ecosystem scanning less predictable.

expected: Plugin authors have a clear naming target.
Discovery and marketplace tooling can prioritize the dreamgraph-plugin-* prefix.
Documentation can present one canonical naming convention.
risks: Prefix squatting or malicious lookalike packages remain possible in public registries.
Some high-quality integrations may use nonconforming names and need explicit allowlisting or aliases.

guard_rails: Use dreamgraph-plugin-* as the canonical public plugin naming convention.
Do not rely on naming alone as proof of trust or safety.
Marketplace and installer flows must still validate manifest, signing or allowlist status, and declared capabilities.

decisions.title: Provider adapters use a hybrid trust model with core presets and signed or allowlisted plugins

context.problem: The SDK roadmap needed to decide how to support provider-specific integrations such as Gemini, OAuth bridges, CLI bridges, and OpenRouter-like providers without contaminating architect-llm or granting unsafe authority to arbitrary plugins.
constraints: architect-llm should remain lean and protocol-pure, consuming normalized LLM/MCP surfaces rather than provider-specific quirks.
Provider adapters may require network access, process execution, OAuth/device-code flows, secrets, retries, and provider-specific error normalization.
Safe/simple OpenAI-compatible providers can often be represented as core presets without a full plugin adapter.
Risky adapters must not receive arbitrary network or process authority by default.

decision.chosen: Use a hybrid provider-adapter model: implement safe/simple providers as core presets; allow risky or complex adapters through signed or allowlisted plugins; never grant arbitrary network or process authority by default. Adapters normalize provider quirks behind a stable LLM/MCP-facing surface so architect-llm stays protocol-pure.

alternatives.option: Put Gemini and other provider-specific behavior directly into architect-llm
alternatives.rejected_because: Would contaminate the architectural reasoning layer with provider-specific request shaping, safety settings, streaming formats, tool-call conversion, auth, and error handling.

alternatives.option: Allow any plugin to perform arbitrary network or process calls as a provider adapter
alternatives.rejected_because: Would violate the SDK trust model and expose secrets, operator environment, and process/network authority too broadly.

alternatives.option: Only support core provider presets and never plugin adapters
alternatives.rejected_because: Would keep the core safer but limit integration with complex providers whose quirks are better isolated in optional adapters.

expected: architect-llm can remain focused on normalized protocol semantics.
Gemini-style integrations can live in adapters that handle provider-specific content parts, tool calls, safety blocks, streaming chunks, model IDs, auth, and errors.
OpenRouter and other OpenAI-compatible providers can start as core presets where possible.
Security review can focus on signed or allowlisted adapters for providers requiring elevated authority.
risks: The normalized provider contract may be hard to design across Gemini, OpenAI-compatible providers, OAuth-backed services, and CLI bridges.
Adapter signing and allowlisting infrastructure must be implemented before broad third-party provider adapters are safe.
Core presets may accumulate too many special cases if not kept strict.

guard_rails: Do not add provider-specific Gemini-style quirks directly to architect-llm without superseding this decision.
Do not grant provider-adapter plugins arbitrary fetch, socket, shell, or child_process authority by default.
Require signed or explicitly allowlisted status for risky provider adapters that need network, process, OAuth, or secret-bearing capabilities.
Keep simple OpenAI-compatible providers as core presets when they do not require new trust boundaries.
Provider adapters must present normalized LLM/MCP-facing requests, responses, tool-call events, stream events, errors, and capability metadata to core consumers.

decisions.title: SDK host loader discovers declared ESM plugins only from instance roots and keeps runtime loading out of M1

context.problem: The SDK roadmap needs a stable host loading model before plugin APIs become public. Without an explicit discovery and module-loading rule, plugin authors and daemon code could depend on accidental paths, CJS/ESM behavior, or early runtime loading semantics that are hard to revoke.
constraints: M1 must ship SDK and host package skeletons without runtime plugin loading.
DreamGraph is a type=module Node project, so ESM should be the default module format.
Plugin discovery must be instance-admin controlled, not implicit global scanning.
Version skew must be handled through manifest engine.dreamgraph ranges before any plugin code executes.
In-process execution is trusted-only until later worker isolation hardening.
related_tensions: SDK packaging must be stable before plugin runtime loading exists

decision.chosen: Use an explicit host loading model: discover plugins only from <instance>/plugins/*/plugin.json and packages listed in instance.json plugins; target ESM modules as the supported plugin format; validate plugin.json and engine.dreamgraph before importing plugin code; keep @dreamgraph/host in M1 as a schema/contract package with no runtime plugin execution; defer in-process loading to the trusted M3 model behind the host safety switch.

alternatives.option: Scan all node_modules packages matching dreamgraph-plugin-* automatically
alternatives.rejected_because: Implicit scanning expands trust and supply-chain risk and conflicts with instance-admin control.

alternatives.option: Support CJS and ESM equally from day one
alternatives.rejected_because: Dual loader semantics create packaging ambiguity before the SDK surface is stable.

alternatives.option: Implement runtime plugin loading in M1
alternatives.rejected_because: M1 is intentionally a skeleton/schema phase; loading before capability gates and audit artifacts are stable would freeze unsafe contracts.

expected: Plugin installation remains explicit and auditable.
M1 can validate package shape and manifests without executing third-party code.
Future M3 loader work has a clear discovery and validation sequence.
ESM-first package design avoids dual-package hazards in the initial SDK.
risks: Some plugin authors may expect automatic npm package discovery.
CJS-only plugin authors will need migration guidance or a later compatibility decision.
Host package may appear underpowered until M3 because it intentionally does not load plugins.

guard_rails: Do not add runtime plugin execution to M1.
Do not discover plugins outside instance-admin declared roots.
Validate manifest schema and engine.dreamgraph before importing plugin main modules.
Keep ESM as the default supported plugin module target unless a later ADR supersedes it.
Do not imply in-process plugin loading is sandboxed before worker isolation exists.

decisions.title: Schedule actions will migrate from a closed union to a guarded registry without changing existing schedule semantics

context.problem: The SDK roadmap requires plugins to eventually register schedule action types, but current schedule behavior depends on known built-in actions, timeout handling, error streaks, and workflow visibility. Opening the action type space without a registry design could break existing schedule semantics or make custom actions unobservable.
constraints: Existing built-in schedule semantics must not change during registry migration.
Timeout and error-streak guards must apply uniformly to built-in and plugin actions.
system://workflows must continue to expose a stable enumerable surface for operators and tools.
Plugin actions must be capability-gated and schema-validated.
M4 implements the seam; M1 should only document and type the eventual contract where needed.
related_tensions: Open plugin seams must not weaken core operational guards
SDK contracts should avoid freezing implementation internals too early

decision.chosen: Adopt a schedule action registry design in which built-ins are first-class registry entries, plugin actions use open string IDs only through explicit registration, every action declares a zod-validated parameter schema, and the scheduler invokes all action types through the same timeout, error-streak, and observability wrapper. system://workflows lists both built-in and registered plugin action metadata while preserving stable built-in identifiers.

alternatives.option: Keep ScheduleAction as a permanently closed union
alternatives.rejected_because: Prevents the planned plugin schedule action seam.

alternatives.option: Allow arbitrary string actions without a registry
alternatives.rejected_because: Breaks validation, observability, and operator trust.

alternatives.option: Give plugin actions a separate scheduler path
alternatives.rejected_because: Would bypass or duplicate timeout/error-streak behavior and create inconsistent semantics.

expected: M4 can open the schedule action seam without bypassing existing protections.
Built-in actions can migrate incrementally into the registry.
Operators retain a discoverable action catalog.
Plugin action failures produce the same telemetry and pause behavior as built-in failures.
risks: Registry migration may reveal assumptions in code that expects a closed union.
Action ID collision rules must be precise to avoid shadowing built-ins.
Schema validation errors need clear operator-facing rejection reasons.

guard_rails: Do not invoke plugin schedule actions outside the shared scheduler guard wrapper.
Do not allow plugin action IDs to collide with built-in action IDs.
Require registered action parameter schemas before accepting a schedule using a plugin action.
Keep built-in action IDs stable in system://workflows.
Do not implement arbitrary string action execution without registry metadata.

decisions.title: M3 plugin host runtime is now active and graph should treat plugin loading as implemented, tested platform capability

context.problem: The project has moved beyond the M1/M2 planning state for plugins. M3 host runtime, stable plugin telemetry contracts, reject reasons, system://plugins inventory, dg plugin CLI, and reference plugin loading are now implemented and tested, but prior graph knowledge and ADR context still emphasize future-tense or host-stub assumptions. The graph must preserve the milestone transition so future reasoning does not continue treating plugin loading as unimplemented.
constraints: Plugin loading in M3 is in-process and trust-gated; it is not a sandbox.
The host runtime is opt-in via allowInProcessPlugins / DG_ALLOW_INPROCESS_PLUGINS and may also require per-plugin trust.
Stable plugin telemetry kinds are host-owned contracts and must remain documented as such.
system://plugins is the canonical operator-visible inventory for loaded/discovered plugins.
Runtime evidence from server logs confirms at least one successful plugin load for examples.hello-events@0.1.0.

decision.chosen: Treat M3 as completed and update graph reasoning accordingly: @dreamgraph/host is an implemented daemon plugin runtime providing discovery, manifest validation, capability/effect gating, telemetry emission, trust banner behavior, watchdog support, system://plugins inventory, and dg plugin administration. Plugin telemetry event kinds and PluginRejectReason are stable SDK contracts. examples/hello-events is the reference plugin and runtime evidence of successful loading should be considered validation input for the feature state.

alternatives.option: Keep graph state at pre-M3 planning/stub status until a later manual documentation sweep
alternatives.rejected_because: This leaves the graph stale and causes future reasoning to misclassify implemented host-runtime behavior as planned-only.

alternatives.option: Treat M3 plugin runtime as production-sandboxed capability
alternatives.rejected_because: The current model is trust-gated in-process execution, not worker-isolated sandboxing; overstating security would be inaccurate.

expected: Future graph queries can rely on plugin host runtime as implemented rather than speculative.
Operator/runtime reasoning can use system://plugins and dg plugin as active surfaces.
Future planning can treat worker isolation and deeper sandboxing as later milestones rather than prerequisites for plugin loading existence.
risks: Some pre-existing graph entities and docs may still contain stale future-tense wording until separately refreshed.
Recording milestone completion via ADR does not by itself rewrite every feature/workflow entity description.

guard_rails: Do not describe M3 plugin execution as sandboxed; it is trust-gated in-process loading until later worker isolation lands.
Do not regress plugin telemetry kinds from stable host-owned SDK contracts without a superseding ADR.
Do not model webhook dead-letter as part of M3 plugin host completion; that remains outside this milestone.

decisions.title: Normalize graph understanding of implemented M3 plugin capability surfaces and workflow

context.problem: The graph now has ADR-137 marking M3 plugin host runtime as active, but feature/workflow-level graph understanding still risks under-specifying the implemented seams. Source evidence shows the concrete implemented capability surfaces are broader and more precise than a single milestone ADR: stable host-owned plugin telemetry kinds in @dreamgraph/sdk, a typed PluginRejectReason taxonomy, a real PluginContext surface with an explicit deny-list posture, host discovery/load gating via allowInProcessPlugins and per-plugin trust, system://plugins as canonical inventory, dg plugin admin commands, and examples.hello-events as validation/reference plugin. Without an explicit normalization decision, future graph reasoning may keep treating these as scattered code details instead of one coherent implemented capability cluster and workflow.
constraints: M3 is an in-process trusted-plugin runtime, not a sandbox; graph wording must preserve that boundary.
system://plugins is the canonical operator-visible inventory and must remain the preferred read surface for loaded/discovered plugin state.
Plugin telemetry event kinds and PluginRejectReason are stable SDK contracts and should not be modeled as experimental or daemon-private.
PluginContext is an API boundary with an explicit deny-list posture; the graph must not infer unrestricted host authority from in-process execution.
Plugin loading remains gated by host allowInProcessPlugins policy and/or explicit per-plugin trust overrides.
examples.hello-events is a reference/smoke-test plugin and runtime validation artifact, not a production capability in itself.
webhook.dead_letter remains outside M3 scope per prior decisions.

decision.chosen: Record that the implemented M3 plugin capability cluster comprises: (1) stable SDK plugin telemetry kinds plugin.loaded / plugin.unloaded / plugin.errored / plugin.handler.started / plugin.handler.completed / plugin.output.accepted / plugin.output.rejected; (2) typed PluginRejectReason taxonomy as the canonical rejection-reason contract shared by SDK and host gates; (3) PluginContext as the developer-facing runtime surface with explicit deny-list semantics and scoped identity/instance/logger/read APIs; (4) a host workflow of discover -> manifest/engine validate -> capability/effect gates -> trust/in-process load gate -> activate -> registry publish -> system://plugins exposure -> dg plugin administration; and (5) examples.hello-events as the reference validation plugin proving discovery/load/inspection behavior. Future graph enrichment should treat these as implemented linked surfaces of one active plugin-host feature family.

alternatives.option: Leave plugin capability understanding implicit across code/docs and rely only on ADR-137 milestone state
alternatives.rejected_because: That leaves the graph semantically shallow and forces future reasoning to rediscover concrete surfaces from source instead of using normalized graph knowledge.

alternatives.option: Model M3 plugin runtime primarily as a sandbox/security feature
alternatives.rejected_because: That would be inaccurate; the implemented boundary is trust-gated in-process loading with API-level deny-list semantics, not a full sandbox.

expected: Future graph queries can consistently answer what the active M3 plugin surfaces are without rereading code.
Plugin discovery/load/rejection reasoning can anchor to a canonical workflow description rather than scattered implementation hints.
SDK and daemon surfaces stay semantically linked: telemetry kinds, reject reasons, gates, registry, inventory resource, CLI, and example plugin.
Later milestones such as worker isolation can supersede parts of this capability cluster without obscuring the M3 baseline.
risks: ADR-level normalization still does not physically create every desired feature/workflow node if generic upsert tools remain unavailable.
Some legacy docs still contain planning-era wording and may need later cleanup to fully match the normalized graph view.

guard_rails: Do not describe M3 PluginContext or host loading as a sandbox boundary; it is a trusted in-process API boundary.
Do not model plugin telemetry kinds or PluginRejectReason as daemon-internal details; they are stable SDK contracts.
Do not treat examples.hello-events as equivalent to a production plugin marketplace or signing model.
Do not collapse system://plugins, dg plugin, and host gating into unrelated features; they are part of one operator-facing plugin runtime family.
Do not pull webhook dead-letter semantics into M3 plugin workflow scope.

decisions.title: DreamGraph v9.0.0 is the released baseline and SDK roadmap M0–M6 is complete, tested, verified, documented, committed, and tagged

context.problem: The canonical DreamGraph graph currently contains plugin-host ADRs up through M3 normalization, but it does not yet explicitly record that DreamGraph v9.0.0 is the released baseline where the SDK roadmap from M0 through M6 is complete and no longer merely planned. Repo and git evidence now show a v9.0.0 tag, release commits, package versions at 9.0.0 for root/sdk/host, release notes stating 'Plugin SDK milestones M0 → M6 (complete)', docs updated to the v9.0.0 baseline, and passing tests covering M4 plugin contributions, M5 outbound webhook/core behavior, M6 UI/closure seams, plugin lifecycle behavior, and hello-events end-to-end validation. Without recording this in the canonical graph, future reasoning may continue to treat late-stage SDK milestones as provisional or infer stale roadmap status.
constraints: The graph record must distinguish verified released baseline status from earlier milestone ADRs that described only subsets such as M3 plugin runtime.
M5 outbound webhooks were intentionally delivered as core platform behavior rather than plugin-owned runtime capability and that scope boundary must remain preserved.
M6 records extensibility seams and host/UI integration contracts without implying a plugin marketplace, sandbox, or signed-distribution model.
The release claim must be grounded in repo evidence: git tag/commits, package versions, release notes, docs, and passing tests.
Earlier ADRs (including ADR-131, ADR-132, ADR-135, ADR-137, ADR-138) remain historically valid and should be interpreted as stepping stones to this released baseline, not contradictions.

decision.chosen: Record DreamGraph v9.0.0 as the canonical released baseline in which the SDK roadmap M0 through M6 is complete, tested, verified, documented, committed, and tagged. Treat the SDK/host capability family as active platform surface rather than roadmap intent: M0 manifest and host loader foundation, M1 dg plugin operator CLI, M2 telemetry/observability contracts, M3 trusted in-process plugin runtime and inventory, M3.5 hot reload and richer introspection, M4 plugin-contributed tools/resources/prompts, M5 outbound webhooks delivered as core-first platform capability interoperating with SDK surfaces, and M6 UI/closure/extensibility seams. Future graph reasoning should use v9.0.0 as the stable baseline unless superseded by a later release ADR.

alternatives.option: Leave v9.0.0 release status implicit in release notes and source only
alternatives.rejected_because: That would force future sessions to re-verify release evidence from files and git rather than relying on canonical graph memory.

alternatives.option: Record only that roadmap work is 'mostly complete' without asserting released baseline status
alternatives.rejected_because: That would understate the verified evidence and preserve stale ambiguity about whether M4-M6 are still roadmap items.

alternatives.option: Model M5 and M6 as plugin-runtime-only milestones
alternatives.rejected_because: That would conflict with the implemented architecture where webhooks are core-first and M6 exposes extensibility seams without implying a broader marketplace/runtime model.

expected: Future graph queries can answer that DreamGraph v9.0.0 is the stable release baseline for SDK/host functionality without re-reading repo evidence.
Roadmap ambiguity is reduced: M0-M6 should be treated as completed/released history rather than active planned work.
Plugin/runtime, webhook, and UI seam discussions can anchor to a single release-baseline ADR that supersedes planning-era assumptions.
Later releases can explicitly supersede this baseline with narrower change-focused ADRs instead of restating completion history.
risks: Some existing feature/workflow nodes may still retain older planning-era wording until separately normalized.
If later patch releases refine contract details, this baseline ADR may need supersession or targeted clarification.

guard_rails: Do not describe SDK milestones M0-M6 as pending roadmap work after v9.0.0 unless a later ADR explicitly reopens scope.
Do not reinterpret M5 as plugin-owned webhook runtime; preserve the core-first webhook boundary.
Do not infer sandboxing, signing, or marketplace guarantees from this release baseline unless separately recorded.
Use v9.0.0 as the authoritative baseline for SDK/host/docs/tests until superseded by a later release ADR.

decisions.title: Architect v2 lives in a parallel folder; main stays shippable until the v10.0.0 cutover commit

context.problem: DreamGraph v9.0.0 "Lattice" just shipped with a working but heavily patched Architect surface (~17000 LOC across ~60 files in extensions/vscode/src/, including a chat-panel.ts.good rollback artifact next to a 3600-LOC chat-panel.ts). A clean rewrite toward v10.0.0 must happen without breaking the released extension on main, without a long-lived feature branch that rots, and without a half-migrated state where v1 and v2 fight over the same files.
constraints: Main must remain shippable at every commit during the rewrite.
No long-lived feature branch is allowed; integration friction would compound over a multi-slice rewrite.
Existing v1 Architect must keep working for users on v9.x throughout the rewrite.
v2 must be free to evolve its internal shape without touching v1 source files.
The cutover from v1 to v2 must be a single auditable event, not a gradual blend.

decision.chosen: Build Architect v2 in a parallel folder at extensions/vscode/src/architect-v2/. The existing v1 Architect surface stays untouched on main and continues shipping in v9.x releases. The v10.0.0 release is defined as the cutover commit that (a) deletes the v1 Architect files enumerated in plans/ARCHITECT_V2_SLICE1_INVENTORY.md §6 and (b) renames extensions/vscode/src/architect-v2/ contents into the canonical positions extension.ts expects. No mixed-mode period; cutover is atomic.

alternatives.option: In-place rewrite of the existing files
alternatives.rejected_because: Would either break main mid-rewrite or require a long-lived feature branch that diverges from main and accumulates merge debt across multiple slices.

alternatives.option: Long-lived feature branch (architect-v2 branch)
alternatives.rejected_because: Multi-slice rewrites on a side branch always rot; merge cost grows nonlinearly and the team loses incremental release leverage.

alternatives.option: Gradual file-by-file replacement on main
alternatives.rejected_because: Creates a half-migrated state where v1 and v2 share file paths, causing tool collisions, prompt collisions, and unclear ownership during the transition.

expected: Main is releasable at every commit during the rewrite — v9.1, v9.2, … can ship intermediate slices behind a feature flag (or stay unreleased) without disturbing v1 users.
The v10.0.0 cutover is a single auditable commit with a precise deletion manifest (plans/ARCHITECT_V2_SLICE1_INVENTORY.md §6).
v2 surfaces evolve freely under architect-v2/ without ever touching v1 source files, eliminating accidental cross-contamination.
Rollback at any point before cutover is trivial — delete architect-v2/ and ship.
risks: Some shared infrastructure (extension.ts, commands.ts, daemon-client.ts, types.ts) must be refactored carefully so that v1 keeps working while v2 grows next to it.
Two near-parallel implementations briefly increase repository size during the rewrite period.
Cutover commit will be large by line count (mass deletes + renames), requiring careful review.

guard_rails: Do not modify v1 Architect source files (the deletion list in plans/ARCHITECT_V2_SLICE1_INVENTORY.md §6) for new feature work during the rewrite — only critical bugfixes.
Do not begin in-place renaming of architect-v2/ contents into the v1 file paths before the formal v10.0.0 cutover commit.
Do not allow v2 code to import from v1 files or vice versa; the two surfaces are isolated until cutover.
Do not introduce a long-lived 'architect-v2' branch; all v2 work lands on main inside extensions/vscode/src/architect-v2/.

decisions.title: v10.0.0 is the cutover release; intermediate Architect v2 slices ship as v9.x behind a feature flag

context.problem: During the multi-slice Architect rewrite, the project still needs a coherent versioning story: when does the version bump, what does v10.0.0 mean, and how are intermediate slices released without confusing users about which Architect they are running?
constraints: Existing v9.0.0 users must keep getting bug fixes and minor improvements during the rewrite.
v10.0.0 must be a clean break, not a 'mostly v2 with some v1 still around' release.
Intermediate releases must not require users to opt into a half-built v2.
Release version semantics must stay predictable — v9.x = v1 Architect, v10.x = v2 Architect, no exceptions.

decision.chosen: v10.0.0 is reserved for the cutover commit. All intermediate Architect v2 progress ships as v9.1.0, v9.2.0, … on main. Each minor v9.x release may include v2 internals behind an off-by-default feature flag (or stay unreleased to npm/marketplace if no user-facing change is ready). v1 remains the default Architect for every v9.x release. The first commit on main that flips the default to v2 and deletes v1 is the v10.0.0 release commit.

alternatives.option: Bump major to v10.0.0 at the start of the rewrite and ship intermediate v10.0.0-rc.N pre-releases
alternatives.rejected_because: Pre-release tags fragment user installs and break the 'main is shippable' invariant for stable release channels; users expect v10.x to be the new Architect, not a half-built one.

alternatives.option: Stay on v9.0.0 for the entire rewrite and bump only at cutover
alternatives.rejected_because: Loses the ability to ship intermediate value (instrumented v2 internals behind a flag, bug fixes to v1, opt-in v2 previews) and concentrates all release risk into one giant version bump.

alternatives.option: Branch v9 maintenance from main and develop v10 on main
alternatives.rejected_because: Contradicts ADR-140's parallel-folder choice and creates the long-lived branch problem we explicitly rejected.

expected: Users on v9.x get a stable Architect throughout the rewrite period.
Each completed Slice can ship as a v9.minor release with v2 internals dark-launched behind a flag, providing real telemetry without changing default behavior.
v10.0.0 marks a single clear product transition — marketing, docs, release notes, migration guide all align to one version.
Internal teams can opt into v2 previews via the feature flag and report regressions early without affecting general users.
risks: A long rewrite period could accumulate many v9.minor releases with growing dark-launched code that never gets exercised by real users until cutover.
The feature flag must be reliable; if it leaks, users on v9.x could accidentally land on v2 internals and report bugs against the wrong codepath.

guard_rails: Do not bump to v10.x.x for any commit before the cutover.
Do not enable the v2 feature flag by default in any v9.x release.
Do not ship a v9.x release that breaks v1 default behavior — v1 is the contract for v9.x.
Do not skip from v9.x straight to v11.x; v10.0.0 must be the cutover release.

decisions.title: Every Architect v2 slice produces both a Markdown plan and ADR mirror(s); the two formats must agree

context.problem: DreamGraph treats ADRs (queryable via mcp_dreamgraph_query_architecture_decisions) as the canonical decision store, but a multi-slice rewrite also needs human-readable narrative documents for review, onboarding, and diff archaeology. The team needs an explicit rule about which format owns what so neither is an afterthought.
constraints: DreamGraph cognitive cycles must be able to reason over rewrite decisions — they live in the graph or they don't exist for the dream engine.
Human reviewers (and the user) read Markdown in the repo; an ADR-only baseline is invisible during code review.
A single source of truth would be ideal but ADR JSON is poor for narrative prose and Markdown is poor for structured graph queries.

decision.chosen: Every Architect v2 slice produces both: (a) a plain Markdown plan/inventory/spec document under plans/ for human review and diffing, AND (b) one or more ADRs recorded via mcp_dreamgraph_record_architecture_decision for graph reasoning. The two formats must agree. The Markdown document is the canonical narrative; the ADRs are the canonical machine-readable decision records. Slice 1 establishes the pattern: plans/ARCHITECT_V2_SLICE1_INVENTORY.md + ADR-140 through ADR-145.

alternatives.option: Markdown file only
alternatives.rejected_because: The graph cannot reason over an external Markdown file; future cognitive cycles, dream insights, and graph_rag_retrieve queries would miss the entire baseline.

alternatives.option: ADR(s) only
alternatives.rejected_because: Humans review plans by reading files in the repo; an ADR-only baseline is invisible during code review and onboarding, and Markdown remains the diff-friendly source for human discussion.

alternatives.option: Auto-generate the Markdown from the ADRs at build time
alternatives.rejected_because: Adds tooling complexity now to solve a problem we don't yet have; the dual-write cost for a single inventory document is trivial, and divergence detection can be added later if needed.

expected: Future dream cycles, tension detection, and graph_rag_retrieve calls can reason over the rewrite using ADR-140… series.
Human PR review and onboarding stays grounded in repo files (plans/ARCHITECT_V2_*.md).
Slice handoffs always cite both the Markdown section and the ADR id, making cross-references unambiguous.
Drift between the two surfaces is detectable by inspection — if a future ADR contradicts plans/ Markdown or vice versa, an explicit reconciliation ADR is required.
risks: Dual-write cost: every locked decision must be expressed twice.
Drift risk: Markdown and ADR can diverge if updated separately; mitigated by guard rails but not eliminated.
Slight ambiguity about which format wins in a contradiction — explicit rule: ADRs win for machine reasoning; Markdown wins for narrative; conflicts trigger a reconciliation ADR.

guard_rails: Do not begin a slice without producing both a Markdown plan/inventory document AND its ADR mirror(s).
Do not silently update one format without updating the other in the same commit.
Do not delete the Markdown plans/ document after recording the ADR — both must persist.
Do not record an ADR whose chosen direction contradicts an existing Markdown plan without first deprecating the Markdown section in the same commit.

decisions.title: Cards are split by responsibility: DreamGraph persists task state, webview owns UI state, cards are views not entities

context.problem: v1 Architect mixes card responsibilities: the webview parses LLM JSON envelopes itself (third copy of extraction logic), some task state is implicit in chat history with no separate record, and cognitive cycles cannot reason over past task outcomes because they are not persisted as graph entities. The team needs a clean split that preserves graph-grounded reasoning while letting the UI evolve freely.
constraints: Task history must survive extension reload, workspace reload, and multi-session work — it is durable evidence.
UI presentation must evolve freely without migrating persisted data.
Cognitive cycles (dreams, tensions, narrative) must be able to reason over past task outcomes.
Webview must not become a parallel parsing surface for LLM envelopes — today's three-extractor problem must not recur.

decision.chosen: Cards are split by responsibility. DreamGraph persists task-state records: decisions taken, blockers encountered, verification evidence, graph-linked context summaries, autonomy pass outcomes, provider+model used, and tool-call results that have lasting value. The VS Code webview owns rendered card UI state: layout, expand/collapse, streaming progress, transient presentation, animation timing, and per-instance preferences. Cards are views over persisted task records, not graph entities themselves. The webview consumes typed events emitted by the orchestrator and never re-parses LLM envelopes directly.

alternatives.option: Cards as full graph entities
alternatives.rejected_because: Couples graph schema to UI presentation churn; every webview redesign would mutate persisted graph data, and the graph would carry rendering noise (collapse states, scroll positions) that has no semantic value.

alternatives.option: Cards owned entirely by webview
alternatives.rejected_because: Loses durable task history; reload, multi-session continuity, and graph-grounded reasoning over past decisions would all be impossible because the webview is ephemeral and unreachable from cognitive cycles.

alternatives.option: Mirror everything to both stores
alternatives.rejected_because: Doubles persistence cost and creates synchronization bugs; every UI tweak risks corrupting graph state and every graph update risks mis-rendering.

expected: Task history is queryable via DreamGraph for audit, narrative, and dream-cycle reasoning.
Webview redesign is a presentation-only change with zero persistence migration.
Single canonical envelope extractor in architect-v2/cards/ — the three-parallel-extractors problem from v1 cannot recur because the webview consumes typed events instead of raw text.
Cards display correctly across all providers, all streaming states, and all partial-response edge cases because rendering reads from a single typed source.
risks: Graph schema must accommodate task-state records (new entity type or extension of existing); requires careful design.
Typed event protocol between orchestrator and webview becomes a stable contract that must be versioned.
Initial implementation cost is higher than 'webview parses everything' but pays back in reliability and graph reasoning.

guard_rails: Do not parse LLM envelopes inside the webview — it consumes only typed events from the orchestrator.
Do not store UI presentation state (collapse, scroll, animation) in DreamGraph.
Do not store durable task evidence (decisions, blockers, verification, provider, model) only in the webview.
Do not introduce a second envelope extractor anywhere in architect-v2/; the canonical extractor lives in architect-v2/cards/.
Do not let webview state and graph task records drift — graph is authoritative for what happened, webview is authoritative only for how it currently looks.

decisions.title: Architect v2 enforces a strict 5-tier execution priority: MCP graph → MCP mutation → MCP verification → VS Code APIs → shell

context.problem: v1 Architect's tool execution layer has implicit precedence between local extension-host tools and MCP daemon tools, with name collisions (local write_file vs MCP create_file, local read_local_file vs MCP read_source_code) and bypass points where v1 reaches for vscode.workspace.fs / vscode.workspace.findFiles when an MCP/DreamGraph tool would be the graph-first choice. Without a structural priority order, graph-first is a slogan, not an invariant.
constraints: Graph-first principle: DreamGraph is the primary context, planning, memory, and safety boundary — reaching around it must be the exception, not the default.
Tool selection must achieve 99.999999% reliability target with no false 'tool unavailable' aborts.
Some operations are genuinely extension-host-only (clipboard, shell, opening editor tabs, accessing user selection) and a pure-MCP rule would be unworkable.
Today's local tools (read_local_file, write_file, modify_entity) duplicate MCP equivalents and create collisions — must be eliminated.

decision.chosen: Architect v2 enforces a single execution priority order that the tool dispatcher must follow for every tool call: (1) MCP entity / API / graph queries, (2) MCP file mutation (create_file, edit_file, edit_entity, patch_markdown_chapter), (3) MCP verification + runtime senses (query_self_metrics, query_runtime_metrics, query_db_schema, etc.), (4) VS Code editor APIs (only when MCP is genuinely inappropriate or absent for the operation), (5) generic shell via run_command. The dispatcher logs the selected tier per call as machine-readable trace. Local 'duplicate' tools (read_local_file, write_file, modify_entity) are removed; only operations that genuinely require the extension host (clipboard, shell, opening editor tabs for the user, document selection) remain at tier 4. Any code path that flips this priority must escalate via a new ADR.

alternatives.option: Keep v1's mixed local+MCP tool registry as-is
alternatives.rejected_because: Today's tool collisions (local write_file vs MCP create_file, etc.) and unclear precedence cause silent behavior changes when MCP availability flips; this is exactly the patch-stacking smell the rewrite must eliminate.

alternatives.option: Pure MCP, no local fallback
alternatives.rejected_because: Some operations (clipboard access, shell execution against the user's workspace) are extension-host-only capabilities that the daemon genuinely cannot provide; a pure-MCP rule would force unnatural detours.

alternatives.option: Let the LLM decide priority case-by-case
alternatives.rejected_because: Violates the 99.999999% tool-selection reliability target; relies on prompt discipline rather than structural enforcement, and the LLM's choice would be invisible to audit.

expected: MCP/DreamGraph is structurally privileged in every tool call; graph-first is enforced by the dispatcher, not by prompt discipline.
Tool-selection trace is machine-readable and auditable per call — future drift is detectable.
Tool collisions disappear because local duplicates of MCP tools are removed; only extension-host-unique operations remain at tier 4.
Adding a new tool requires explicit tier assignment, making the priority order self-documenting.
risks: Some MCP tools may have higher latency than local equivalents; users may notice slower file operations. Mitigation: cache hot reads at the dispatcher tier, not at the tool tier.
Tier 4 boundary judgments (when is VS Code API genuinely required?) need consistent enforcement during code review.
Removing local duplicates means MCP availability becomes a hard dependency; daemon down = degraded experience. Mitigation: clear UX signal when MCP is unreachable.

guard_rails: Do not call a VS Code editor API for an operation an MCP tool can perform.
Do not reintroduce local duplicates of MCP file-mutation tools (write_file, edit_file, edit_entity, etc.).
Do not bypass the dispatcher to call a tool directly — all calls flow through the prioritized registry.
Do not skip the tier-trace log for any tool invocation.
Do not flip the tier order for a single call without recording a new ADR.

decisions.title: Architect v2 locks local provider flagships: LM Studio = gpt-oss-120b high-context, Ollama = qwen2.5-coder:32b

context.problem: v1 Architect leaves local provider model selection entirely to user settings, which produces ambiguous first-run behavior for LM Studio and Ollama users and complicates documentation, benchmarking, and troubleshooting because there is no canonical 'recommended' model per provider.
constraints: Local-first deployments need a sensible flagship default per provider; first-run experience with no model picked is poor.
LM Studio and Ollama have different runtime characteristics; a single shared default would be wrong for at least one.
User explicitly chose these flagships during the rewrite kickoff and locked them as the v2 baseline.
Cloud provider defaults must stay aligned with the v9.0.0 locked set (GPT-5.5/5.4, Claude 4.7 xhigh).

decision.chosen: Architect v2 ships with locked local provider flagships: LM Studio default model = gpt-oss-120b in high-context configuration. Ollama default model = qwen2.5-coder:32b. These are the recommended defaults baked into the provider profile model; users override per-instance via settings, but the out-of-box experience uses these flagships. Cloud provider defaults (already locked in v9.0.0): OpenAI = GPT-5.5 Responses API as default + GPT-5.4 previous API as equal-class option; Anthropic = Claude 4.7 xhigh.

alternatives.option: Leave local provider defaults as 'whatever the user has installed'
alternatives.rejected_because: Settings ambiguity wastes user time; first-run experience with LM Studio or Ollama is poor when no flagship is recommended, and the user explicitly asked for locked defaults.

alternatives.option: Make local providers a single shared default
alternatives.rejected_because: LM Studio and Ollama have different runtime characteristics and different best-in-class models; a shared default would be wrong for at least one of them.

alternatives.option: Auto-detect installed local model and pick the best one at runtime
alternatives.rejected_because: Adds discovery logic and surprise; users prefer predictable defaults they can override over magic that might pick the wrong model.

expected: First-run experience with LM Studio or Ollama is predictable: a flagship is selected, user knows what to download.
Provider profile model can ship validated capability flags for these specific defaults (context window, tool-call format, reasoning support).
Documentation, troubleshooting, and benchmark suites can target known defaults rather than 'whatever the user picked'.
Users override defaults per-instance via VS Code settings; the lock is only for out-of-box experience.
risks: Recommended local flagships may become outdated as new models release; superseding ADR will be required when bumping defaults.

User hardware may not support the flagship (gpt-oss-120b high-context needs significant VRAM); UX must clearly signal hardware requirements and provide fallback guidance without silently switching models.

guard_rails: Do not change the LM Studio default away from gpt-oss-120b high-context without a superseding ADR.
Do not change the Ollama default away from qwen2.5-coder:32b without a superseding ADR.
Do not change cloud provider defaults (GPT-5.5 Responses API + GPT-5.4 previous API + Claude 4.7 xhigh) without a superseding ADR.
Do not silently fall back to a different local model when the flagship is unavailable — surface the gap clearly so the user can install or override.

decisions.title: Architect v2 Slice 1 demolition baseline: full v1 surface inventory + per-slice handoff contracts

context.problem: The Architect v2 rewrite needs a verified, exhaustive baseline of what exists in v1 today \u2014 every file, every smell, every Copilot-parity gap, every MCP-bypass point, every migration risk \u2014 so future slices can be grounded in evidence rather than memory or assumption, and so the v10.0.0 cutover commit has a precise deletion manifest. Without this baseline, the rewrite would inherit v1's patch-stacking by accident.
constraints: Rewrite must not assume v1 internals — must be grounded in a verified read-only inventory.
User explicitly required no assumptions and no shortcuts; demolition map must be exhaustive.
Cutover commit at v10.0.0 must have a precise file-deletion list to be auditable.
All future slices must be able to cite specific inventory sections as their input — no implicit dependencies.
Inventory must agree across Markdown (plans/) and ADR (graph) representations per ADR-142.

decision.chosen: Slice 1 of the Architect v2 rewrite produces a complete demolition baseline for the v1 Architect surface (~17000 LOC across ~60 files in extensions/vscode/src/), captured in plans/ARCHITECT_V2_SLICE1_INVENTORY.md and mirrored as ADR-140 through ADR-146. The inventory enumerates: (a) per-surface current-state map covering chat path, cards, autonomy, providers, tool execution, context engine, memory/continuity, prompts, and webview; (b) ranked patch-stacking smells (top severity: three parallel envelope extractors causing the user-visible 'summaries render as JSON and autonomy stops working' bug); (c) Copilot-parity gaps to close in v2; (d) MCP-bypass points violating the graph-first principle; (e) migration risks for future slices to plan around; (f) precise deletion manifest for the v10.0.0 cutover commit; (g) target shape skeleton for architect-v2/ directory. Slice 1 closes when the architect-v2/ skeleton exists with empty placeholders and a README referencing this ADR. All subsequent slices (2 through 7) consume specific sections of this inventory as their declared input.

alternatives.option: Skip the inventory and start writing v2 code
alternatives.rejected_because: Without a demolition map, v2 risks accidentally reproducing v1 smells (parallel envelope extractors, dual budget systems, hardcoded magic numbers); the user explicitly rejected assumptions and shortcuts.

alternatives.option: Build v2 incrementally without a final cutover deletion list
alternatives.rejected_because: Leaves a half-migrated state where v1 and v2 share file paths; ADR-140 already rejected this. The deletion list is the contract that makes the cutover commit auditable.

alternatives.option: Inventory only the smelliest files (chat-panel.ts, autonomy-*)
alternatives.rejected_because: Partial inventory would miss the cross-cutting smells (three trimming layers, two budget systems, three envelope extractors) that only become visible when the full surface is mapped.

expected: Every v2 slice has a verifiable input contract pointing at specific inventory sections; no slice begins on assumption.
The v10.0.0 cutover commit has a precise deletion manifest — ~35 v1 source files identified for removal.
Three top-severity user-visible smells (parallel envelope extractors, dual autonomy analysis, three trimming layers) are explicitly tagged for elimination in slices 3, 4, and 5.
MCP-bypass points are catalogued so slice 4 can systematically reroute them through the dispatcher.
Cross-cutting risks (persisted-schema drift, tool collisions, envelope drift) are pre-identified so slices can build mitigations from the start, not discover them late.
risks: Inventory may miss subtle implicit contracts that only surface during slice implementation — reconciliation ADRs will be required as discoveries happen.
v1 may receive bugfix changes during the rewrite that drift the deletion manifest; mitigated by guard rail requiring explicit list maintenance.
Inventory document is large; future readers must navigate by section rather than reading top-to-bottom.

guard_rails: Do not start a v2 slice without citing the specific inventory section(s) it consumes.
Do not modify plans/ARCHITECT_V2_SLICE1_INVENTORY.md after Slice 1 close without recording a reconciliation ADR.
Do not let the deletion manifest in inventory §6 drift from reality — if a v1 file is added after Slice 1, decide explicitly whether it joins the deletion list.
Do not declare any v2 slice complete until both its Markdown plan and its mirroring ADR(s) exist per ADR-142.
Do not skip Slice 1's architect-v2/ skeleton scaffolding step — it is the closure condition for Slice 1.

decisions.title: Architect v2 providers are profile records in a registry; orchestrator depends only on the ProviderAdapter contract

context.problem: Architect v1 routes provider-specific behavior through switch statements inside `ArchitectLlm`, hardcodes model capability flags, and parses tool-call envelopes in multiple places. Inventory \u00a71.4, \u00a72 row 6, and \u00a75 row \"Provider model-list rot\" identify this as a structural cause of the two-OpenAI-paths smell, the silent reasoning-effort header risk, and adapter divergence. v2 needs a uniform abstraction that the orchestrator and autonomy engine can depend on without ever knowing which provider is active.
constraints: Architect v2 must remain provider-agnostic at the orchestrator layer; provider quirks may not leak past the adapter boundary.
Adding or removing a provider must be a single registry change, not a switch-case surgery across multiple files.
Tool-call reliability target (99.999999% per inventory §3) requires the canonical tool-call shape to be defined once and translated by adapters, not parsed in multiple places.
Strict isolation from v1 — no `import` and no copy-paste of v1 provider code (locked at Slice 2 kickoff).

decision.chosen: Architect v2 models providers as `ProviderProfile` records in a registry rather than a class hierarchy. Each profile declares: its `id` (closed enum), `displayName`, `modelSource` ('static' or 'discovery'), `defaultModelId`, `listModels()`, and `createAdapter(model, config)`. Each model is a `ModelDescriptor` with declarative `ModelCapabilities` (api discriminator, streaming, toolCallShape, attachments, reasoning support, maxOutputTokens). The orchestrator depends only on the `ProviderAdapter` contract (`stream`, `callWithTools`) and the canonical request/response/event/error shapes \u2014 it never branches on provider id at the wire layer. Slice 2 ships the types + registry + stub adapters that throw `ProviderAdapterNotImplementedError`; real adapters land in later slices behind the v2 feature flag.

alternatives.option: Keep v1's class-based ArchitectLlm shape and just rebuild internals
alternatives.rejected_because: v1's switch-statement provider routing is the root cause of the two-OpenAI-paths smell and the silent reasoning-effort header mismatch risks documented in inventory §1.4 and §5; a per-provider record-based registry is what makes ADR-148 (one OpenAI provider, model-driven dispatch) implementable cleanly.

alternatives.option: Use a third-party LLM router library (LangChain.js / Vercel AI SDK)
alternatives.rejected_because: Adds a heavy runtime dependency, hides the provider quirks behind another abstraction we'd still have to debug, and conflicts with the rewrite principle of owning the wire layer end-to-end for token economy and tool-call reliability.

alternatives.option: Defer the registry until after a working adapter exists
alternatives.rejected_because: Slice 3+ work (autonomy, execution) needs a stable seam to depend on; without the registry contract, every later slice would re-invent its own adapter abstraction and we would re-create v1's tangled state.

expected: Future slices implement their own logic against the `ProviderAdapter` contract; they can be developed and tested with mock adapters before any provider is wired.
Adding a fifth provider (e.g. xAI, Google) becomes a single new profile file plus one registry entry, not a refactor of `ArchitectLlm`.
The two-OpenAI-paths smell from v1 inventory §2 row 6 is structurally precluded — model.capabilities.api is the single source of truth for wire format.

Capability flags drive request shaping declaratively; the silent reasoning-effort header risk from inventory §5 cannot recur because unknown effort levels are caught by `ReasoningSupport.effortLevels` enforcement at the adapter boundary.
risks: The canonical `ChatRequest` / `StreamEvent` / `ToolCall` shapes must absorb every provider's quirks; a future provider with truly novel semantics may force a backwards-incompatible widening.

Stub adapters are runtime-throwing; if a code path accidentally instantiates a stub during Slice 2 work it will fail at the call site (mitigated: feature flag remains off and stub adapters are easy to recognize in stack traces).
Discovery-source providers (LM Studio, Ollama) ship Slice-2 placeholder lists; consumers that enumerate models must understand this is not yet the real list.

guard_rails: Do not branch on `ProviderId` inside the orchestrator or autonomy engine — branch on `ModelCapabilities` fields.
Do not introduce a provider-specific request type that bypasses `ChatRequest`; adapters translate from the canonical shape, not from a per-provider one.
Do not parse provider-specific tool-call envelopes anywhere except the corresponding adapter; the rest of v2 sees only `ToolCall`.
Do not throw provider-raw errors past the adapter boundary; every failure must be wrapped in `ProviderError` with a closed-enum `kind`.
Do not ship a provider adapter without the corresponding `ModelCapabilities` flags being honored end-to-end (streaming, toolCallShape, reasoning, attachments).

decisions.title: Single 'openai' provider; ModelCapabilities.api selects Chat Completions vs Responses API per model

context.problem: v1 ships two parallel OpenAI code paths \u2014 standard Chat Completions in `architect-llm.ts` and Responses API in `openai-responses-adapter.ts`. Inventory flags this as a HIGH-MEDIUM duplication smell. v2 must support both APIs (because gpt-5.5 requires Responses API while older models still use Chat Completions) without reproducing the dual-path problem.
constraints: v1's two parallel OpenAI paths (architect-llm.ts standard route + openai-responses-adapter.ts) are a HIGH-MEDIUM smell in inventory §2 row 6; v2 must not reproduce them at the provider-id level.
Users select a model, not an API; the UX must match.
OpenAI's roster includes both Chat Completions models and Responses-API-only models simultaneously, so a single-API-per-provider model is incorrect.
The dispatch decision must be declarative on the model descriptor, not buried inside adapter code.

decision.chosen: Architect v2 exposes ONE `openai` provider entry. Each model's `ModelCapabilities.api` field is the discriminator that selects between OpenAI Chat Completions and OpenAI Responses API at request time. Slice 2 wires gpt-5.5 with `api: 'openai-responses'` and gpt-5.4 with `api: 'openai-chat-completions'`. The orchestrator never sees an 'OpenAI mode' selector; users pick a model, and the model's metadata routes the request.

alternatives.option: Two distinct providers: 'openai-chat' and 'openai-responses'
alternatives.rejected_because: Splits the OpenAI surface in the settings UI and forces users to think about which API a model uses; this is exactly the cognitive leak ADR-148 exists to remove. It also recreates the v1 two-paths smell at a higher level.

alternatives.option: Hardcode an api branch inside one OpenAI adapter implementation (no capability flag)
